4 C PK C  |  U nited S tates Air B rake and Train H andling
1.0 G eneral Requirements
1.1 Compliance w ith F RA Regulations
Inspect and test brake equipment on locomotives and cars according to F ederal R ailroad Administration 
(F R A) regulations contained within these rules. This is the responsibility of the employee(s) who perform 
the work, unless otherwise instructed.
1.2 Q ualified P ersonnel
A Q ualified Person or a Q ualified Mechanical Inspector may perform inspections and air brake tests.
1.3 P erson in Charge of Air Brake T est
The person performing the air brake test is in charge of the train while the test is being conducted. B efore 
permission is given to apply or release the brakes, the person in charge must determine that all crew 
members are safely positioned.
The employee controlling the locomotive must not apply or release train brakes or move the train without 
permission from the person performing the air brake test.
1.4 Brake T est G eneral Requirements
B efore performing any train air brake test complete the following:
• Properly position all angle cocks and valves.
• Ensure retaining valves are in EX  (Direct Exhaust) position.
• C ouple the brake pipe air hoses .
• R elease hand brakes unless required for securement.
• Ensure the rear car is charged to a minimum of 7 5-psi .
• If using the Air F low Method, the Air F low indicator(s) must be calibrated.
1.5 Handheld G auges
H andheld air gauges need to be verified as accurate to within + / - 3 - psi. Accuracy can be verified by 
connecting the handheld air gauge to the brake pipe air hose of a locomotive and comparing the pressure 
against the locomotive brake pipe gauge. If the pressure displayed on the handheld gauge exceeds 
tolerance, it must not be used. H andheld gauges must be tested annually for accuracy . 
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 5
2.0 Air Hoses 
2.1 Coupling and Securement
When coupling air hoses employees must:
• Prior to coupling, check for and remove foreign matter and blow condensation from the brake 
pipe hose.
• Verify that the brake pipe glad hands are at least 5 inches above the top of the rail.
• When equipped, ensure air hose supports are connected.
2.2 Use of Adapter Hoses
The following requirements will apply to the use of adapter hoses:
• Adapter hoses must not be used when departing an initial terminal unless authorized 
by Mechanical.
• Where required enroute, only use an adapter hose to move equipment to the next terminal where 
inspections and repairs can be made.
3.0 Charging the Brake System
3.1 Air Brake System Charge Requirements
The air brake system must be charged to the pressure(s) required by this section.
A handheld gauge or EOT located at the rear of a train may be used to determine that the air brake 
system has been charged to a specified pressure and brake pipe pressure has been restored. A 
distributed power consist located at the rear of a train may be used to determine that flow is within 
specified limits and brake pipe pressure has been restored.
Do not charge a train’s air brake system with more than one automatic brake valve cut in unless utilizing 
distributed power. If unable to maintain a minimum main reservoir pressure of 105-psi, the throttle may be 
advanced to notch 4 with the generator field switch open. This does not apply to locomotives equipped 
with an electronic air compressor.

6 CPK C |  U nited States Air Brake and Train H andling
4 .0 Train Brake Pipe Leakage Tests
4 .1 Leakage Test Required
Brake pipe leakag e must be tested when conducting  Class I or Class IA air brake tests. The Air F low 
Method is the preferred method to test brake pipe leakag e.
4 .2 Air F l ow Method (AF M)
To utiliz e the AF M,  a train must be equipped with the following :
• A 26 -L or equivalent pressure maintaining  automatic brake valve.
• Operative Air F low Indicator with a direct reading  of air flow in increments no g reater than 10 
cubic feet per minute ( CF M) .
• Operational H OT and EOT or handheld g aug e.
Perform the AF M test as follows:
• Charg e the air brake system to 75-psi.
• U sing  the AF M indicator,  ensure air flow does not ex ceed:
o 6 0 CF M for conventional trains .
o 9 0 CF M combined air flow with no more than 6 0 CF M at any consist for distributed power 
trains.
• If CF M ex ceeds limits above,  inspect the train for leakag e,  make necessary repairs,  
and retest.
4 .3  Brake Pipe Leakage Test (N on - AF M)
If an AF M test cannot be performed,  conduct the following  test:
• Ensure the brake system is charg ed to at least 75- psi.
• W ait for the sig nal to apply the brakes .
• W hen sig nal is received,  make a 20- psi reduction with the automatic brake.
• Allow the brake pipe ex haust to stop.
• W ait 6 0 seconds .
• Cut out the automatic brake.
• W ait an additional 6 0 seconds .
• D o not actuate the independent brake or move the automatic brake handle until test is complete.
• Time brake pipe leakag e for 6 0 seconds.
o If brake pipe leakag e does not ex ceed 5- psi,  test is complete.
o If brake pipe leakag e ex ceeds 5 -psi,  inspect train for leakag e,  make necessary repairs,  
and retest.
• W hen a sig nal to release the brakes is received,  move the automatic brake handle to the release 
position and cut in the automatic brake valve.

sections.title: 8 CP K C |  U nited S tates Air Brake and Train H andling
sections.text:
8 CP K C |  U nited S tates Air Brake and Train H andling
6 .0 Air Brake S tatus
6 .1 O p erativ e Brakes
Air brakes must be operative on 100 percent of cars at the initial terminal. Cars qualified by a Class IA or 
transfer test and cars picked up enroute, must have 100 percent operative brakes unless properly tagged 
and approved by a Q ualified M echanical Inspector. 
At least 8 5 percent of the cars in a train must have operative brakes. 
6 .2 Inop erativ e Brakes
Air brakes on all cars must be operative, except:
• Cars with air brakes that fail enroute may be handled to the next forward repair location.
• When properly tagged by a Q ualified M echanical Inspector, cars may be moved for repair under 
the following air brake tests:
o Class I, at locations other than the initial terminal.
o Class IA.
o Transfer.
N o more than two consecutive cars in a train may have inoperative brakes. 
The rear three cars of a train must have operative brakes. If the rear car’ s air brakes become inoperative 
enroute, movement may continue under the direction of M echanical as follows:
• Test the hand brake on the disabled car.
o If the hand brake is inoperative, do not move the car until repaired.
• Chain, strap, or cable the disabled car to the adj acent car.
• Ensure the brake pipe is connected and open between the disabled car and train.
o If necessary to close the angle cock on the disabled car, ensure the angle cock on the 
adj acent car remains open.
 This will ensure that an emergency brake application can propagate throughout the train 
in the event the disabled car becomes separated.
• M ove the car directly to the first available location where it can be switched between cars with 
operative brakes or set out of the train.
Cars with inoperative brakes must be reported to M echanical and recorded on the Crew Information 
F orm. 
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 9
7.0 Class I Air Brake Test
7.1 Class I Air Brake Test Requirements
Conduct a Class I air brake test on a train:
• Where the train is originally assembled.
• When the train has been off air for more than 24 hours.
• When a train is received in interchange or a location where the train consist is changed other 
than by:
o Changing locomotive consist.
o Adding a previously tested car or solid block of cars.
o Removing a car or solid block of cars.
o Removing defective equipment.
o Any combination of the changes listed above.
• A unit or cycle train has traveled 3,000 miles since its last Class I.
Conduct a Class I air brake test on a portion of a train:
• When car(s) have been off air for more than 24 hours.
• When one or more cars are added to a train that have not been pretested by a Class I air brake 
test.
• When a solid block of cars are added to the train that are comprised of cars from more than one 
previous train.
• When a car or solid block of cars from a single previous train have not remained continuously and 
consecutively coupled with the train line remaining connected, except:
o When cars are separated into multiple solid blocks due to space or trackage constraints.
 Cars must be recoupled in the same order as removed.
7.2 Class I Air Brake Test Procedure
To perform a Class I air brake test, complete the following:
• Charge the air brake system to at least 75-psi.
• Test brake pipe leakage.
• When signal is received, make a 20-psi reduction with the automatic brake.
o Brakes must remain applied for a minimum of three minutes and until a 
release initiated.
o If test is unsuccessful, retest cars until compliant or set out of train.
 Brakes must be operative on 100 percent of cars.
• Verify brakes apply on each car, brake rigging does not bind or foul, and piston travel is within 
applicable limits.
• Inspect each side of each car to examine and observe the functioning of all moving parts of the 
brake system and comply with the freight car inspection requirements.
o Equipment must be stationary during the inspection.
• When signal is received, move the automatic brake handle to release.
• Inspect each car and verify that brakes are released.
o Release may be verified during a roll-by inspection, not exceeding 10 mph.

7 .3  E ng ineer N otification
The locomotive engineer must be notified with the results of a Class I air brake test. This information must 
be recorded on the Crew Information F orm or electronic record and retained in the controlling locomotive 
cab until the train reaches its destination.
At minimum, notification will include:
• Test completion status.
• Date and time.
• L ocation of test .
• N umber of cars inspecte d.
• N ame of person(s) performing test .
8 .0 Class IA Air Brake Test – 1, 000 M ile Insp ection
8 .1 Class IA Air Brake Test Procedure
To perform a Class IA air brake test, complete the following:
• Charge the air brake system to at least 75-psi.
• Test brake pipe leakage.
• When signal is received, make a 20-psi reduction with the automatic brake.
o Brakes must remain applied for a minimum of three minutes and until a 
release initiated.
o If test is unsuccessful, retest cars until compliant or set out of train.
o Brakes must be operative on 1 00 percent of cars except as outlined by Operative Brakes of 
this section.
• Verify brakes apply on each car, brake rigging does not bind or foul, and piston travel is within 
applicable limits.
• Inspect each side of each car to examine and observe the functioning of all moving parts 
of the brake system and comply with the freight car inspection req uirements.
o Eq uipment must be stationary during the inspection.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 11
9.0 Class III Air Brake Test  
9.1 Class III Air Brake Test Requirements
Conduct a Class III air brake test on a train:
• When a locomotive consist is changed.
• Adding or removing a car or solid block of cars.
• Adding locomotive(s) to a train after receiving a brake test from a yard air source.
• Adding or removing distributed power or helper locomotive(s) from anywhere in a train.
• When a caboose is added or removed.
9.2 Class III Air Brake Test Procedures
To perform a Class III air brake test, complete the following:
• Charge the air brake system to at least 75-psi.
• Make a 20-psi reduction with the automatic brake.
• Distributed power trains must follow Train Check procedures.
• Verify the brakes apply on the rear car.
o A 5-psi decrease on EOT or rear of train distributed power locomotive can be used to 
determine the brakes are applied.
• Move the automatic brake handle to release.
• Verify the brakes release on the rear car.
o A 5-psi increase on EOT or rear of train distributed power locomotive can be used to 
determine the brakes are released.
When an EOT or rear of train distributed power locomotive cannot be used, the rear car must be visually 
inspected to determine application and release of the brakes.
10.0 Transfer Train Air Brake Test
10.1 Transfer Air Brake Test Requirements
A transfer test may be used on a train movement that does not exceed 20 miles in one direction. 
10.2 Transfer Air Brake Test Procedures
To perform a Transfer Train Air Brake Test, complete the following:
• Charge the air brake system to at least 75-psi.
• When signal is received, make a 20-psi reduction with the automatic brake.
• Verify the brakes apply on each car and remain applied until a release is initiated.
o Brakes must apply on each car, except as outlined by Operative Brakes in this section.

sections.text:
12 CPK C |  U nited S tates Air Brake and Train H andling
11.0 Ex tended H aul  Trains
11.1 Ex tended H aul  Train Requirements
Trains designated as E xtended H aul may be operated greater than 1,000 miles but cannot exceed 1,500 
miles before a subsequent Class I or Class IA air brake test is performed. 
The following requirements apply to E xtended H aul Trains:
• Air brake test and inspection must be performed by a Q ualified Mechanical Inspector .
• The train may not depart an initial terminal with mechanical defects or inoperative brakes.
• The train may not make more than one pick up and more than one set out between the initial 
terminal and intermediate inspection point.
o This does not apply to defective equipment set out enroute.
• Any car or solid block of cars added enroute must be pretested by a Q ualified 
Mechanical Inspector.
12.0 Running Air Brake Test
12.1 Passenger Trains
Perform a Running air brake test on passenger trains and trains consisting entirely of business 
cars when:
• The train leaves the initial terminal.
• L ocomotive, engine crew, train crew, or operating ends have been changed.
• Any angle cocks or cutout cocks have been opened or closed.
• An initial terminal air brake test has been conducted.
• The train reaches points designated by the timetable or general order.
• The train has struck debris on the track.
12.2 Al l  Trains
Conduct a running air brake test when:
• Inclement weather conditions are present which may cause snow or ice build-up to occur 
between the brake shoes and wheels.
• S now is above the top of the rail or where icing conditions may exist and train is approaching:
o A meeting, passing, or stopping point.
o A signal indication which will require the train to stop.
The following requirements apply to running air brake tests:
• The locomotive engineer must make a brake pipe reduction sufficiently in advance of prescribed 
locations to determine that the brakes are working properly.
• If braking effort is not sufficient, the train must be stopped by a full service brake application using 
full dynamic brakes, consistent with proper train handling.
• If deemed necessary, the locomotive engineer must make an emergency brake application 
without hesitation.
• After stop is made, the train must be inspected to determine if brake rigging and shoes are free of 
snow and ice before proceeding.
• Immediately after proceeding, perform a running brake test at a safe speed to determine if the 
brakes respond as intended.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 13
12.3 Running Air Brake Test Procedures
To perform a Running Air Brake Test, complete the following:
• When speed reaches a level adequate to ensure continued motion, make an automatic brake 
reduction sufficient to create an evident retarding force.
• Validate that train brakes are responding as intended.
• If brakes are operating properly, release the automatic brake and proceed.
If the Running Air Brake Test fails, complete the following:
• Immediately stop the train.
• Make a walking inspection of the train to identify issues with the braking system.
• When issues are identified, correct the problem(s) and notify the train dispatcher.
• Before proceeding, perform a Class III air brake test.
• After proceeding, perform another running brake test.
13.0 Enroute Brake Pipe Pressure Requirements
An enroute train must be stopped and inspected for leaks at the next available location when air flow or 
gradient do not return to the following parameters within a reasonable amount of time. The following 
requirements apply:
• Conventional trains:
o Brake pipe gradient must not exceed 15-psi.
o When qualified by an AFM test, air flow must not exceed 60 CFM.
• Distributed Power trains:
o Combined total air flow must not exceed 90 CFM or 60 CFM at any locomotive consist.
In the event a brake application cannot be propagated or an abnormal change or loss in brake 
pipe pressure occurs with the automatic brake released, the train must be immediately stopped 
and inspected.
14.0 Overcharged Brake Conditions
An overcharged brake system occurs when brake equipment on cars or locomotives is charged to a 
higher pressure than the regulating valve setting. 
To eliminate an overcharge on a train:
• Make a full service reduction with the automatic brake.
• Wait two minutes.
• Move the automatic brake handle to release.

sections.title: 14 CPK C |  United States Air Brake and Train Handling
sections.text:
14 CPK C |  United States Air Brake and Train Handling
15 .0 Bl ock Swap s
A Class I Air test is not req uired to be performed on a solid block of cars intended for block swap when 
the solid block of cars is comprised of cars from a single previous train and have:
• Previously received a Class I brake test.
• Remained continuously and consecutively coupled together with the train line connected since 
being removed from the previous train.
• Not been off air for more than 2 4  hours .
Additional req uirement s:
• A freight car inspection must be performed at the location where the car( s)  are added to the train.
• The solid block of cars from a previous train must have the req uired train brake status information 
recorded on a Crew Information Form.
16 .0 Y ard Air
16 .1 Y ard Air Requirements
The following instructions govern the use of yard air systems. Employees are prohibited from using yard 
air sources until proper training has been completed and a clear understanding of respective components 
has been demonstrated.
16 .2 Connecting Y ard Air
To connect yard air:
• Ensure eq uipment is secured.
• Uncouple from the eq uipment to be left standing.
• To ensure the yard air hose remains visible to employees, route the yard air hose through the 
side of the car being connected using a handhold or other location.
• Couple the air hose connection between the cars and yard air system.
• Ensure the angle cock on the eq uipment coupled to the air source is open.
• Open the valve on the yard air source.
16 .3 D isconnecting Y ard Air
To disconnect yard air:
• Prior to coupling to eq uipment, ensure yard air hoses are not positioned in a manner that will 
cause them to be damaged.
• V erify eq uipment is properly secured and couple to eq uipment .
• Close the angle cock on the eq uipment that is coupled to the yard air line.
• Close the air supply valve from the yard air line.
• Release the pressure from the hose connecting the yard air source to the eq uipment .
• Once pressure has been exhausted, remove the air hose from the cars.
• L eave the yard air line in a manner that will not create a tripping haz ard or be damaged 
by eq uipment .
• Couple the brake pipe between eq uipment .
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 15
• Once the locomotive engineer acknowledges the brake system is charged and it is safe to do so, 
release the hand brakes.
• Perform a Class III air brake test.
17.0 Interchange Requirements
17.1 Trains Entering the United States of America (USA) from Canada
Trains which are destined for the USA must have 100 percent operative brakes from the initial terminal or 
an enroute safety inspection location. No train will be permitted to operate into the USA with less than 85 
percent operative brakes. Cars destined for the USA with inoperative brakes or any other safety defect 
must not be moved beyond the first location where repairs can reasonably be made.
17.2 Trains Entering Canada from the USA
Trains may enter Canada when the Crew Information Form indicates a Class l or Class lA 
air brake test has been performed.
17.3 Trains Received from Foreign Carrier
Trains received from a foreign carrier must have the train brake status information transferred to the Crew 
Information Form. The air brake information received from a foreign carrier will be kept with the Crew 
Information Form. In the event train brake status information is unavailable, contact the train dispatcher.
18.0 Crew Information Form and Train Brake Status
18.1 Crew Information Form
The Crew Information Form consists of the following sections:
• EOT Test information:
o Contains a record of train identification, lead locomotive, and EOT test information.
• Defects:
o Portion of form to record locomotive defects.
• Dynamic Brake Status Chart:
o Contains dynamic brake status information.
• Hot Box Detector Information.
• Results of Inbound Train Inspection.
• Emergency Brake Application Inspection Report.
• Train Brake Status:
o Contains information related to initial air brake tests and work performed enroute.

1.0 Car Inspection
1.1 Car Inspection Requirements
At each location where a freight car is placed in a train and mechanical forces are not on duty for the 
purpose of inspecting freight cars, the freight car shall, as a minimum, be inspected for the following 
conditions:
• Car body:
o Leaning.
o Sagging downward.
o Improperly positioned truck.
o Object dragging below.
o Object extending from side.
o Door insecurely attached.
o Broken or missing safety appliance.
• Lading leaking from a placarded hazardous material car.
• Insecure coupling device.
• Overheated wheel or journal.
• Broken or cracked wheel.
• Brake that fails to release.
• Any other apparent safety hazard likely to cause an accident or casualty before the train arrives 
at its destination.
This inspection must be performed on each side of all cars.
2.0 Freight Car End, Platform, and Wheel Identification
2.1 Car End Identification
Identify car ends as follows:
• On cars with one hand brake, the “B” end of the car is the end with the hand brake and the other 
end is the “A” end.
• On cars with more than one hand brake, the letters “A” and “B” are stenciled on the appropriate 
ends of the car.
2.2 Wheel Identification
Car wheel numbers are identified as follows:
• Axles are designated from the “B” end of the car with number 1 being the axle closest to the “B” 
end.
• Wheels and journals are designated as either left or right as viewed from the “B” end.
• Specific wheels are identified using both the axle and wheel designation.

Identify the wheels of a multi- platform car as follows:

2.3 P latform Identification
Identify platforms as follows:

• The “B ” platform is located on the “B ” end of the car, while the “A” platform is located on the “A” 
end.

immediately adj acent to the “B ” end.

3.0 Coupler Identification
3.1 Coupler Assembly Types

is marked with a letter indicating its type, E, F, or H. Knuckles are not interchangeable.

Identify the wheels of a multi- platform car as follows:
• Ax les are designated from the “B ” end of the car with the number 1  ax le closest to the 
“B ” end.
• W heels and j ournals are designated as either left or right as v iewed from the “B ” end.
• S pecific wheels are identified using the ax le and wheel designation.
• W heels will be designated using number 1  through 9  and then alphabet characters from 
“Z ” to “A” for each subsequent ax le.
2.3 P latform Identification
Identify platforms as follows:
• Multi- platform cars hav e stencils indicating “A” and “B ” ends of the equipment.
• The “B ” platform is located on the “B ” end of the car, while the “A” platform is located on the “A” 
end.
• The remainder of the platforms are identified as “C ” through “E” beginning at the platform 
immediately adj acent to the “B ” end.

sections.text:
2 2 CPK C |  U nited S tates A ir B rake and Train H andling
4 .0 Retaining  Valves
4 .1 Retaining  Valve L ocation
The retaining valve controls brake cylinder pressure exhaust on a freight car. A ll freight cars have 
retaining valves located at the “B ” end of the car or on the side near the control valve.
4 .2 Th ree-Position Retaining  Valve
The three-position retaining valve consists of the following positions:
• E xhaust (E X ) – A llows unrestricted passage of brake cylinder pressure to exhaust to atmosphere;
H andle is turned down.
• H igh Pressure (H P) – R estrict the exhaust of brake cylinder pressure at a controlled rate and 
retains 2 0 pounds of brake cylinder pressure; H andle is 4 5  degrees below horiz ontal .
• S low D irect (S D ):  R estrict the exhaust of brake cylinder pressure at a controlled rate to provide a 
blow down time of approximately 86 seconds and continues to exhaust until all brake cylinder 
pressure is vented to atmosphere; H andle is 4 5  degrees above horiz ontal .
4 .3 F our -Position Retaining  Valve
The four-position retaining valve includes the positions listed above and one additional position:
• L ow Pressure (L P):  E xhausts brake cylinder pressure to 10- psi; H andle is horiz ontal.
4 .4  Retaining  Valve U se
The normal position for a retaining valve is D irect E xhaust. When retaining valves are required, the H igh-
Pressure setting must be used and movement must not exceed 2 0 mph.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 23
5.0 Piston Travel
5.1 Piston Travel Requirements
Follow the piston travel requirements outlined on the car’s stencil, sticker, or badge plate. When required, 
this information will be displayed on each side of the car body in a location near the brake cylinder. If no 
stencil, sticker, or badge plate is available, piston travel must be within the following guidelines.
5.2 Body-Mounted Brake Cylinders
• Initial Terminal
o Piston travel on cars equipped with 8 ½ or 10-inch diameter brake cylinders must be 6 to 9 
inches; piston travel outside of this range must be adjusted to 7 ½ inches.
o Cars not equipped with 8 ½ or 10-inch diameter brake cylinders must be within the limits 
indicated on stencil, sticker, or badge plate.
• Intermediate locations
o Piston travel on cars equipped with 8 ½ or 10-inch brake cylinders must be 
6 to 10 ½ inches.
o Piston travel on cars not equipped with 8 ½ or 10-inch diameter brake cylinders must be 
within the limits indicated on stencil, sticker, or badge plate. For maximum travel, use the 
“Piston Travel Ineffective in excess of” column on brake travel stencil.
5.3 Truck-Mounted Brake Cylinders
Piston travel must be within the limits of the travel indicator when brakes are set and provide brake shoe 
clearance when brakes are released.
6.0 Vent Valve
The number 8 vent valve (on the control valve) transmits emergency brake pipe reductions. If the vent 
valve fails to reset after an emergency brake application, causing a continuous blow at the exhaust port, 
plug the valve by removing the vent protector and screwing in the threaded plug.

24 CP K C |  U nited S tates A ir B rake and Train H andling
7 .0 Cu tting O u t A ir B rak e Eq u ipment
Car air brakes may only be cut out in the when brake equipment is defective. To cut out control valves,
close the branch pipe cut out cock and drain the air reservoirs completely by operating the brake cylinder 
release rod. 
8 .0 B leeding Rail Cars
Cars may only be bled off when making repairs to the brake system, cutting out defect cars, 
or switching. 
9 .0 F lat Wheels and S hell S pots – F reight Cars
While inspecting freight car wheels, measure and report as follows:
• Determine the length of the flat or shelled area.
• Notify the Dispatcher and Mechanical when the flat spot or shelled area exceeds 1 inch.
• U se the table below to determine if equipment restrictions apply.
10.0 Towing Eq u ipment
10.1 G eneral Req u irements
The following will apply to the use of tow cables:
• Equipment may only be towed under the direction of Mechanical.
• Mechanical will be responsible to apply tow cables and other required components.
• When uncertainty exists regarding the safe movement of a car with a tow cable, the equipment 
must be moved with a locomotive.
• Do not stand near a tow cable while in use.
• Tow cables must not be connected to axles or truck side frames.
• Except for multi-platform cars, do not attempt to tow more than one car at a time.
• When possible, apply a light hand brake to the car being towed to avoid slack action and shock 
loading of the tow cable.
• While towing, an employee must be in position to operate the hand brake of the car being towed, 
unless doing so would place the employee in the vicinity of the tow cable.

• Trackside Warning Detector alarms and details of inspections.
• Emergency brake applications.
• Train inspection results.
• Location and number of hand brakes applied.
• Details of equipment with inoperative air brakes.
• Details of defective equipment being moved in the train.

28 CP K C |  U nited States Air B rak e and Train H andling

30 CPK C |  U nited S tates Air B rake and Train H andling
sections.text:
30 CPK C |  U nited S tates Air B rake and Train H andling
1.0 G eneral Requirements
Locomotive engineers must ensure:
• Each locomotive in service is inspected at least once during each calendar day.
• Car body compartment, engine room, and end doors of locomotive(s) are closed when not in use.
• O n unoccupied locomotives:
o Awnings are down.
o Mirrors are pulled in.
o Windows and doors are closed.
• H igh voltage cabinets remain closed.
When locomotive(s) are in motion, personnel may only move from one locomotive to an adjoining 
locomotive when:
• A job briefing has been performed concerning:
o Movement between locomotives.
o Required speed to ensure safe passage.
• B oth locomotives are equipped with walkways.
• S afety chains are connected and provide a continuous barrier.
• If there is doubt our uncertainty regarding safe passage, movement between locomotives is 
prohibited.
Employees are restricted from opening engine covers and electrical cabinet doors unless authorized or 
required in the case of emergency.
In case of fire to locomotives or rail diesel cars, engines and fuel pumps should be stopped, emergency 
fuel cutoffs tripped, and battery switches opened as soon as possible.
Locomotives and rail diesel cars must not be stopped over flame type switch heaters. If unavoidable, 
switch heaters must be turned off by the dispatcher or equipment promptly moved. 
2 .0 Locomotive O rientation and W heel N umb ering
The front of the locomotive is designated by the letter “ F”  stenciled on each side of the locomotive. 
Wheels are numbered consecutively as illustrated in the following diagram.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 31
3.0 Standard Air Pressures
The following standards air pressures apply:
• With the automatic brake cut in and in the release position, the main reservoir pressure must be 
at least 15-psi higher than the standard locomotive brake pipe pressure.
• The standard equalizing reservoir pressure setting is 90-psi.
• With independent brake handle fully applied, the brake cylinder pressure must be within 
3-psi of the pressure posted in the locomotive cab.
o If the brake cylinder pressure is unknown, contact Mechanical for instructions.
4.0 Taking Charge of Locomotive(s)
When taking charge of locomotive(s), the locomotive engineer must:
• Determine the locomotive daily inspection status and perform a locomotive daily inspection, if 
required.
• Perform a locomotive air brake test, if required.
• Evaluate the operating condition of locomotive(s).
• Confirm that total driving axle and dynamic brake factors do not exceed the permissible limits and 
record information on the Crew Information Form.
• Ensure that the locomotive air brake system is properly conditioned.
• Ensure that the headlights, ditch lights, bell, and whistle are working on the controlling 
locomotive.
• Ensure the locomotive brakes and devices for regulating air pressures, including the automatic 
and independent brake valves, are operating as intended.
• Check locomotive fuel level(s) and report to the proper authority when fuel levels 
are below:
o 1,000 gallons on road locomotives.
o 300 gallons on yard locomotives.
• Record locomotive defects on the Crew Information Form and report to Mechanical.
An inbound locomotive engineer must conduct a job briefing with the outbound locomotive engineer 
regarding the condition of locomotive(s). If a job briefing cannot be conducted, the condition of 
locomotive(s) must be recorded on the Crew Information Form. 
5.0 Locomotive Daily Inspection
5.1 Inspection Requirement
Locomotive engineers are responsible for determining if locomotive(s) need to be inspected by reviewing 
the Locomotive Daily Inspection Report in each locomotive cab. The card will indicate the date and time 
of the last inspection. Locomotive engineers must ensure that each locomotive in their charge, including 
locomotives picked up enroute, are inspected each calendar day the locomotive is in service. A calendar 
day is comprised of the time between 00:01 and 23:59 hours. The Locomotive Daily Inspection Report on 
the controlling locomotive may be used to determine the inspection date for all locomotives in the train.

sections.text:
32 CP K C |  United S tates Air B rake and Train Handling
5.2 I ns pec ted P rev iou s  Calendar D ay
If the Locomotive Daily Inspection R eport indicates that the locomotive was inspected the previous 
calendar day, then complete the current daily inspection before the end of the tour of duty. Contact the 
train dispatcher, yardmaster, or other proper authority to determine where to complete the daily 
inspection. The locomotive engineer may be relieved from requirements to perform a daily inspection 
when informed by the proper authority that Mechanical or the relieving locomotive engineer will inspect 
the locomotive( s) .
When possible, perform locomotive daily inspections during daylight hours or at the beginning of 
a shift. 
5.3  N ot I ns pec ted P rev iou s  Calendar D ay
If the Locomotive Daily Inspection R eport indicates that the locomotive was not inspected during the 
previous day, or if there is no record on the locomotive, inspect the locomotive before it is placed in 
service on the current day. When not used, the words “ Not Used”  must be written on each applicable date 
line of the Locomotive Daily Inspection R eport.
5.4  L oc omotiv es  P ic ked U p or S et O u t Enrou te
Locomotives picked up enroute must not have an inspection date that precedes the inspection date of the 
controlling locomotive. Locomotives set out enroute must have a current calendar day inspection. The 
locomotive engineer may be relieved from requirements to perform a daily inspection when instructed by 
the proper authority.
5.5 I ns pec tion I tems
Unless functioning properly, the following inspection items will be considered non-complying defects.
5.5.1  L oc omotiv e Cab
From the locomotive cab, ensure: 
• FR A Form F 6 1 80 -4 9A ( blue card)  is displayed and up to date.
• Cab seats are securely mounted and braced.
• Cab doors are equipped with a device to secure the door.
• Cab windows of the lead locomotive provide an undistorted view of the right-of-way for the crew 
from their normal position in the cab.
• Cab floors, passageways, and compartments are free from oil, water or any obstruction that 
creates a slipping, tripping or fire haz ard, and floors have been properly treated to provide secure 
footing.
• The cab of the lead locomotive provides proper ventilation with a heating arrangement that 
maintains a temperature of at least 6 0 degrees Fahrenheit 6  inches above the center of each seat 
in the cab.
• Each air gauge registers within 3-psi of the required pressure.
• A controlling locomotive operating at speeds greater than 2 0 mph has an operative speed 
indicator.
• Locomotive is equipped with a fusee container.
• Cab lights provide sufficient illumination for control instruments and gauges.
• At least one head light is operational on each end of the locomotive consist.
• B oth ditch lights on the leading end of the controlling locomotive are operational .
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 33
• All traction motors are cut in.
o This does not apply to GE-8 DC, GE-9DC, and all AC locomotives.
• The dynamic brake, if equipped, has not been defective for more than 30 days.
• Horn and bell operate on the lead locomotive.
• The locomotive toilet facility is sanitary and operational, if equipped. A locomotive may continue in 
lead with a defective or unsanitary toilet facility when all of the following conditions are met:
o The unsanitary or defective condition is discovered at a location where there are no other 
suitable locomotives available for use.
o The locomotive, while non-compliant, did not pass through a location where it could have 
been cleaned, repaired, or switched with another compliant locomotive since its last daily 
inspection.
o Upon reasonable request of a crewmember operating with a defective or unsanitary toilet 
facility, arrangements are made for the crew to access a sanitary toilet facility outside of the 
locomotive.
5.5.2 Walkway, Car Body, and Engine Compartment
From the walkway, car body, and engine compartment, inspect both sides of each locomotive 
to ensure: 
• Walkways and walk-in compartments are clear of debris, tools, and accumulated 
oil or grease.
• Handrails, handholds, steps, ladders, safety chains, and guards are secured and ready 
for service:
o Inspect for broken, bent, damaged, or loose equipment.
o Make sure safety chains are connected high enough for safe passage.
o No passageway is required through the nose of a car body locomotive.
o Locomotives with open platforms not coupled to another locomotive must have a continuous 
barrier across the full width of the end of a locomotive.
o Locomotive with an open platform coupled to another locomotive without an open platform 
must have a continuous barrier between locomotives.
• All electrical and rotating equipment guards are in place.
• The diesel engine has no apparent exhaust, oil, water, or fuel leaks.
• Locomotive hand brake is operational.

32 CP K C |  United S tates Air B rake and Train Handling
5.2 I ns pec ted P rev iou s  Calendar D ay
If the Locomotive Daily Inspection R eport indicates that the locomotive was inspected the previous 
calendar day, then complete the current daily inspection before the end of the tour of duty. Contact the 
train dispatcher, yardmaster, or other proper authority to determine where to complete the daily 
inspection. The locomotive engineer may be relieved from requirements to perform a daily inspection 
when informed by the proper authority that Mechanical or the relieving locomotive engineer will inspect 
the locomotive( s) .
When possible, perform locomotive daily inspections during daylight hours or at the beginning of 
a shift. 
5.3  N ot I ns pec ted P rev iou s  Calendar D ay
If the Locomotive Daily Inspection R eport indicates that the locomotive was not inspected during the 
previous day, or if there is no record on the locomotive, inspect the locomotive before it is placed in 
service on the current day. When not used, the words “ Not Used”  must be written on each applicable date 
line of the Locomotive Daily Inspection R eport.
5.4  L oc omotiv es  P ic ked U p or S et O u t Enrou te
Locomotives picked up enroute must not have an inspection date that precedes the inspection date of the 
controlling locomotive. Locomotives set out enroute must have a current calendar day inspection. The 
locomotive engineer may be relieved from requirements to perform a daily inspection when instructed by 
the proper authority.
5.5 I ns pec tion I tems
Unless functioning properly, the following inspection items will be considered non-complying defects.
5.5.1  L oc omotiv e Cab
From the locomotive cab, ensure: 
• FR A Form F 6 1 80 -4 9A ( blue card)  is displayed and up to date.
• Cab seats are securely mounted and braced.
• Cab doors are equipped with a device to secure the door.
• Cab windows of the lead locomotive provide an undistorted view of the right-of-way for the crew 
from their normal position in the cab.
• Cab floors, passageways, and compartments are free from oil, water or any obstruction that 
creates a slipping, tripping or fire haz ard, and floors have been properly treated to provide secure 
footing.
• The cab of the lead locomotive provides proper ventilation with a heating arrangement that 
maintains a temperature of at least 6 0 degrees Fahrenheit 6  inches above the center of each seat 
in the cab.
• Each air gauge registers within 3-psi of the required pressure.
• A controlling locomotive operating at speeds greater than 2 0 mph has an operative speed 
indicator.
• Locomotive is equipped with a fusee container.
• Cab lights provide sufficient illumination for control instruments and gauges.
• At least one head light is operational on each end of the locomotive consist.
• B oth ditch lights on the leading end of the controlling locomotive are operational .
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 33
• All traction motors are cut in.
o This does not apply to GE-8 DC, GE-9DC, and all AC locomotives.
• The dynamic brake, if equipped, has not been defective for more than 30 days.
• Horn and bell operate on the lead locomotive.
• The locomotive toilet facility is sanitary and operational, if equipped. A locomotive may continue in 
lead with a defective or unsanitary toilet facility when all of the following conditions are met:
o The unsanitary or defective condition is discovered at a location where there are no other 
suitable locomotives available for use.
o The locomotive, while non-compliant, did not pass through a location where it could have 
been cleaned, repaired, or switched with another compliant locomotive since its last daily 
inspection.
o Upon reasonable request of a crewmember operating with a defective or unsanitary toilet 
facility, arrangements are made for the crew to access a sanitary toilet facility outside of the 
locomotive.
5.5.2 Walkway, Car Body, and Engine Compartment
From the walkway, car body, and engine compartment, inspect both sides of each locomotive 
to ensure: 
• Walkways and walk-in compartments are clear of debris, tools, and accumulated 
oil or grease.
• Handrails, handholds, steps, ladders, safety chains, and guards are secured and ready 
for service:
o Inspect for broken, bent, damaged, or loose equipment.
o Make sure safety chains are connected high enough for safe passage.
o No passageway is required through the nose of a car body locomotive.
o Locomotives with open platforms not coupled to another locomotive must have a continuous 
barrier across the full width of the end of a locomotive.
o Locomotive with an open platform coupled to another locomotive without an open platform 
must have a continuous barrier between locomotives.
• All electrical and rotating equipment guards are in place.
• The diesel engine has no apparent exhaust, oil, water, or fuel leaks.
• Locomotive hand brake is operational.

3 4 C P K C  |  U nited States Air B rake and Train H andling
5.5.3  G rou nd  I nspection
F rom the ground level, inspect both sides of each locomotive to ensure: 
• Sand is deposited on the rail in front of the lead wheels on each locomotive in consist.
o A locomotive being used in switching service at a location not equipped with a sand delivery 
system may continue in service for seven calendars from the date the sanders are found to 
be inoperative or the next periodic inspection, whichever occurs first.
• The fuel tank is not leaking.
• No defects such as cracked, broken, or missing parts are on the following:
o Locomotive trucks.
o Wheels.
o Draft gears.
o G ear cases .
• B rake cylinder piston travel must be as follows:
o Minimum:  Sufficient to provide brake shoe clearance when the brakes are released.
o Maximum: 1 ½  inches less than the travel entered on F RA F orm F  6 18 0 -4 9 A (blue card).
• F oundation brake rigging is secured and all components other than wheels and sand hoses are at 
least 2 ½  inches above the top of the rail.
• B rake shoes are secured and approximately in line with the tread of the wheel and there are no 
obvious lips or overhangs.
• No part of the electrical j umper cable is lying on the coupler.
• U nused electrical cables must be stowed properly or the disconnected ends placed into a dummy 
receptacle or a multiple-unit cable holder.
• C able and cable connections between locomotives may not have broken or badly chafed 
insulation, broken plugs, receptacles, or terminals, or broken or protruding strands of wire.
• The coupler does not have a crack or break in the pulling face of the knuckle.
• Snowplow, pilot, or end plate is properly, secured and is between 3  and 6  inches above the top of 
the rail.
• Main reservoirs are drained of oil and water at least once per day.
• Automatic drain valve handles are turned fully clockwise to the automatic position with the stem 
extending beyond the valve handle, if equipped.
5.6  R ecord ing Daily I nspection
A written report of the inspection shall be made on the Locomotive Daily Inspection Report or other 
equivalent foreign carrier form. The following information must be included:
• Time.
• Location.
• Description of non-complying defects.
• Signature of Inspector.
• Non-complying repairs:
o Description of repairs.
o Signature of person making repairs.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 35
5.7 Tagging Non-Complying or Defective Locomotives
When a non-complying condition or other defect is identified, prior to moving the locomotive(s), complete 
the following:
• Report condition or defect to Mechanical and other proper authority.
• Record the required information on a locomotive defect tag.
o Identify defect type by checking the applicable box (non-complying or defect).
o Locomotive initials and number.
o Name of the inspecting railroad.
o Inspection location and date.
o Nature of defect(s).
o Movement restrictions, if any.
o Destination.
o Signature of the employee making the inspection.
• Attach the locomotive defect tag to the isolation switch of the non-complying or 
defective locomotive.
• Attach a copy of the locomotive defect tag on the control stand of the controlling locomotive.
• The locomotive engineer in charge of the movement must receive written notification of the non-
complying locomotive; a copy of a locomotive defect tag meets this requirement.
o The locomotive engineer must inform all other crew members of the non-complying 
locomotive and of any restrictions.
A locomotive defect tag is not required provided the locomotive is being moved as a single locomotive or 
dead in a yard for the purpose or repair at a speed not exceeding 10 mph.
5.8 Movement of Non-Complying Locomotives
5.8.1 Locomotives Safe to Move
During the locomotive daily inspection if one or more non-complying defects are identified, a locomotive 
may be moved if it is determined by a qualified person the locomotive is safe to move.  If the locomotive is 
safe to move, it may only be moved:
• As a single unit under power not attached to cars.
• In a locomotive consist not attached to cars.
• Isolated or shut down when attached to cars.
• After a locomotive defect tag is completed and attached to the isolation switch.
Exceptions:
• A controlling locomotive with a defective speed indicator identified during a daily inspection may 
be operated under power attached to cars not exceeding 20 mph.
• Locomotive(s) found with the following defects during the daily inspection may be operated under 
power attached to cars as a trailing locomotive:
o Inoperative headlights or ditch lights.
o Inoperative horn or bell.
o Defective speed indicator.
o Window cracks that obscure view.
o Improperly secured cab seats.

o I noperative safety devices.

5 .8 .2 Locomotives N ot Safe to Move
During the locomotive daily inspection if one or more non- complying defects are identified and the 
locomotive( s)  are not safe to move:
• R eport the condition or defect to Mechanical and other proper authority.
• C omplete a locomotive defect tag and attach as required.
5 .8 .3  N on-C omplying C ondition( s)  Found E nroute
A  locomotive that develops a non- complying condition enroute may continue in service provided the 
locomotive engineer or other qualified employee determines that the locomotive is safe to move. T he 
locomotive may be operated until the next daily inspection or the nearest point where repairs can be 
made, whichever comes first. T he locomotive engineer must:
• R eport the condition or defect to Mechanical and other proper authority.
• R ecord the defect information on the C rew I nformation F orm .
• C omplete the locomotive defect tag and attach as required.
• Notify the relieving locomotive engineer of non- complying conditions.
5 .8 .4  Defects O ther Than N on-C omplying C onditions
I f a defect other than a non- complying condition ( bad order) is found during a daily inspection or while 
enroute, the locomotive engineer must:
• R eport the condition or defect to Mechanical and other proper authority.
• R ecord the defect information on the C rew I nformation F orm .
• C omplete the locomotive defect tag and attach as required.
5 .8 .5  Major I nternal Defects Found E nroute
I f a locomotive develops a maj or internal defect enroute, comply with the following:
• I mmediately shut down the engine.
• R eport the condition to the train dispatcher and Mechanical .
• Do not restart the engine unless instructed by Mechanical.
• C omplete the locomotive defect tag and attach as required.
• I f instructed to set out the defective locomotive, when possible, leave in a location that can be 
accessed by Mechanical.
I f safe to do so, a dead locomotive may continue as a controlling locomotive until the next daily inspection 
or the nearest point where repairs can be made, whichever comes first.

• Determine the length of the flat or shelled area.
• Notify the dispatcher and Mechanical when the flat spot or shelled area exceeds 1 inch.

7.0 Dynamic Brake Requirements
On train movements equipped with dynamic brakes, the controlling locomotive must:
• Have the ability to control the dynamic brakes on trailing locomotives in the consist, if equipped 
and operative.
• Be equipped with either an operative dynamic brake or accelerometer that displays current 
change in speed or predicted change in speed in miles per hour per minute.

sections.title: 38 CPK C |  United States Air B rake and Train H andling
sections.text:
38 CPK C |  United States Air B rake and Train H andling
8.0 Driving Axle Req uirements
8.1  G eneral Restric tions – All T rains
The following general driving axle restrictions will apply to all trains:
• No more than 28 driving axles are permitted in the lead consist of loaded crude oil trains.
• No more than 24 driving axles are permitted in the lead consist of trains handling DO T 111 tank 
cars.
• No more than 16 driving axles are permitted on trains operating over tracks where 6 axle 
locomotives are prohibited.
8.2 Driving Axle L imitations – Conventional T rains
Unless otherwise specified by this section or other instruction, a conventional train must not exceed 30 
driving axles. The following exceptions apply:
T rAM  Areas 1 ,  2 ,  and  3
Trains are permitted to operate with up to 36 driving axles when the following conditions are met:
• The head 15 cars must weigh at least 50 tons.
• When multi-platform cars are part of the head 15 cars, no platforms can be empty and the 
average weight of all platforms on each car must be 50 tons or more.
• When energy management is active, manual control must be taken when tractive effort exceeds 
100 K lbs as indicated by the lead locomotive.
• When operating at speeds below 12 mph, do not exceed the following tractive effort levels as 
indicated by the lead locomotive:
o 135 K lbs when operating with 30 to 35 driving axles .
o 110 K lbs for 36 driving axles .
T rAM  Are as 4,  5 ,  and  6
The following driving axle requirements will apply:
• Do not exceed 24 driving axles.
8.3 Driving Axle L imitations – Distrib uted  P ow er T rains
The maximum number of driving axles permitted on distributed power trains are as follows:
T rAM  Areas 1 ,  2 ,  and  3
• Lead Consist: 30.
• In-train R emote(s): 12.
• R ear R emote: 12 .
T rAM  Areas 4,  5 ,  and  6
• Lead Consist: 24.
• In-train R emote(s): 12.
• R ear R emote: 12 .
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 39
Additional locomotives may be included in remote consists provided they are isolated. 
The driving axle limits above may only be exceeded when an approved configuration is listed in the 
Distributed Power Placement chart. In the case of doubt or uncertainty, crew members must contact 
management for guidance.
8.4 Driving Axle Ratings
Driving axle ratings are as follows:
• 4 driving axles:
o All 4 axle locomotives (except GP60).
• 6 driving axles:
o GP60.
o SD30.
o SD40.
o SD50.
• 8 driving axles:
o D-8, D-9, D-9-40CW, D-944CW.
o SD60.
o SD70 (Non ACU models).
• 12 driving axles:
o AC4400.
o ES44AC.
o SD70AC.
o SD90.
When the driving axle rating of a locomotive is unknown, the following will apply:
• 4 axle locomotives – 6 driving axles.
• 6 axle DC locomotives – 8 driving axles.
• 6 axle AC locomotives – 12 driving axles.
9.0 Coupler Alignment Control
Unless otherwise specified:
• All leased locomotives will be equipped with coupler alignment control.
• All private industry locomotive(s) and the CP 6711 must be marshalled in-train.
Locomotives without coupler alignment must be marshalled as follows:
• As part of the lead consist:
o Marshall immediately behind the lead locomotive.
o If no locomotive is marshalled immediately behind the locomotive without coupler alignment 
control, the first two cars of the train must be no less than 65 feet and weigh at least 45 tons.
• As part of the train:
o Comply with requirements for handling dead or disabled locomotives in a train.

4 0 CPK C |  United S tates A ir Brake and Train Handling
10.0 Placement of  Dead or Disabled Locomotives
10.1 Placing Dead/ Disabled Locomotives B ehind Lead Consist ( Pref erred M ethod)
Dead or disabled locomotives may be coupled directly behind the lead consist provided:
• E ach locomotive is equipped with coupler alignment control .
• Locomotive(s) are conditioned using the dead engine cut out cock under the direction of the 
mechanical department (as required).
• Movements are governed by any restrictions and/ or instructions placed by the Mechanical 
Department.
10.2 H andling Dead/ Disabled Locomotives in T rain ( Alternative M ethod)
Dead or disabled locomotives, including locomotives without coupler alignment control, which cannot be 
placed within the lead consist, may be placed in-train provided:
• Passes TrA M check.
• Locomotive(s) are conditioned using the dead engine cut out cock under the direction of the 
Mechanical department (as required).
• N o more than two dead/ disabled locomotives are marshalled in-train .
• Movements are governed by any restrictions and/ or instructions placed by the Mechanical 
department.
A  single locomotive with a damaged drawbar must be positioned to the extreme rear of a train and may 
be moved provided:
• Passes a TrA M check .
• The locomotive is conditioned using the dead engine cut out cock under the direction of the 
Mechanical department (as required).
• A ir brakes are operative.
• Movements are governed by any restrictions and/ or instructions placed by the Mechanical 
department.
11.0 Cold W eather Operation – H igh Idle
When the ambient temperature is expected to be at or below 0 °  F ahrenheit, prior to being left unattended, 
locomotives not equipped with high idle protection must be throttled up manually.
To manually throttle up a locomotive:
• G enerator F ield Off .
• Control/ F uel Pump and E ngine R un On.
• R everser Centered.
• Throttle advanced to notch 4 .
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 41
12.0 Draining a Locomotive
During cold weather operation, when a locomotive is shut down and cannot be restarted, the engine 
cooling water must be drained as outlined by the draining instructions posted in the cab. When in doubt, 
contact Mechanical for guidance.
When draining engine cooling water, ensure all people are clear of the cooling water drainpipe pressure 
relief outlet and the filler pipe connector.
13.0 Starting and Stopping Locomotives
Procedures to start and stop locomotives are posted within the locomotive cab or starting station. If 
required, contact Mechanical for assistance.
14.0 Isolating Locomotives
The following will apply when isolating locomotive(s):
• While in motion, the isolation switch of a lead locomotive must be in the run position 
at all times.
• Unless otherwise specified, light engine consists may only operate with one locomotive 
on-line.
• While a locomotive is under load, do not place the isolate switch to run or isolate.
15.0 Response to Alarms
Locomotive alarms must be investigated as soon as possible. If a continuous wheel slip, pinion slip, or 
locked axle indicator is displayed, stop the movement immediately and contact Mechanical for 
instructions.
16.0 Crankcase Overpressure
Do not restart a locomotive that has shut down due to crankcase overpressure. Contact Mechanical for 
guidance.
17.0 Locomotive Power Limit Switch
If equipped, the power limit switch (HP Boost) must be on at all times.
18.0 Snowblaster and Rail Cleaner Operation
On locomotives equipped, compressed air is used to clean snow and debris from the rail. The cleaning 
device is installed near each lead axle sand bracket on the front of the locomotive and may be activated 
automatically or manually.

sections.title: 42 CPK C |  U nited States Air B rake and Train H andling
sections.text:
42 CPK C |  U nited States Air B rake and Train H andling
19 .0 F ire Prevention
19 .1 Preventing  Sp ark s
L ocomotives that idle for extended periods of time may discharge sparks from the exhaust stack. 
To reduce the possibility of sparks on stationary locomotives that have been idling for extended periods, 
perform the following:
• Center the reverser.
• Advance the throttle to notch 5 for 10  minutes.
While operating, train crews must be alert to evidence of excessive spark emission from the locomotive(s) 
or train.
19 .2 L ocomotives Susp ected of Starting  F ires
Whenever possible, shut down locomotive(s) that are suspected of starting fires. This information must be 
recorded on the Crew Information Form and reported to Mechanical.
20.0 Electronic D isp lay  Screen F ailure on L ead L ocomotive
On conventional trains, if one display screen fails, the locomotive may continue in service. If both screens 
fail, the locomotive must be repaired or removed from the lead position. On distributed power trains, if one 
or both screens fail, the locomotive must be repaired or removed from the 
lead position. 
All screen defects must be promptly reported to Mechanical.
21.0 Event Recorder and C amera Sy stems
Access to event recorder and camera systems is restricted. Only authorized personnel may extract event 
recorder and camera data. The camera system must be on and unobstructed at all times. Any action 
which interferes with the normal operation of the event recorder or camera system will be subj ect to 
discipline.
22.0 L ocomotive Safety  D evices
L ocomotive safety devices must be cut in and operating at all times. 
This requirement does not apply to the following:
• N on -controlling locomotives.
• D istributed power locomotive(s).
• D ead -in-tow locomotives.
Safety device malfunctions must be immediately reported to Mechanical and other proper authority. D o 
not cut out, tamper with, or defeat a safety device without proper authorization. 
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 43
23.0 Alerters
23.1 Alerter Requirements
All controlling locomotives that operate at speeds greater than 25 mph must be equipped with an 
operative alerter. If the alerter malfunctions enroute, then the locomotive engineer must:
• Immediately notify the dispatcher and document the malfunction on the Crew 
Information Form.
• Contact and be governed by Mechanical’s instructions for cut out of the alerter.
A locomotive with an inoperative alerter may continue to operate as a controlling locomotive until the next 
daily inspection or forward point where repairs can be made.
23.2 Test Procedure
To test the alerter on a locomotive, complete the following:
• Protect the locomotive(s) from unintended movement.
• Initiate a penalty brake application by placing the automatic and independent brake handles in the 
release position and allowing the alerter to time out.
• Ensure the audible alarm and warning lights are functioning properly.
• Ensure equalizing reservoir pressure reduces to 61-psi or lower.
• Recover the penalty brake application.
23.3 Alerter Nullification
When required to temporarily nullify the alerter for loading and unloading unit bulk trains, the following will 
apply:
Standard Procedure
These steps will nullify the alerter at speeds of 2 mph or less:
• Move throttle to Idle.
• Center reverser.
• On distributed power trains, place remote consist(s) in remote mode Idle.
• Isolate the controlling locomotive.
• Release the independent brake.
Alternate Procedure (to be Used When Standard Procedure is Not Effective)
These steps will nullify the alerter at speeds of 4 mph or less:
• Isolate all locomotive in the lead consist, except the controlling unit.
• On distributed power trains, place remote consist(s) in remote mode Idle.
• Select slow speed control on the operator screen.
• Set slow speed control to zero or lowest speed possible if zero is unavailable.
• Move the reverser to the direction of travel.
• Advance throttle to notch 1.
• Isolate lead locomotive.
• Release the independent brake.

sections.title: 4 4 CPK C |  U nited S tates Air B rake and Train Handling
sections.text:
4 4 CPK C |  U nited S tates Air B rake and Train Handling
24 .0 Locomotive S p eed  I nd icators
A locomotive used as a controlling unit at speeds above 2 0 mph must be equipped with an operative 
speed indicator. If a speed indicator on a controlling locomotive fails enroute, it must be handled as a 
non-complying condition found enroute. The locomotive may continue in the lead position at maximum 
authoriz ed speed until the next calendar day inspection or next repair facility, whichever occurs first.
The speed indicator must be tested for accuracy as soon as possible after leaving a terminal using 
measured miles or other equivalent procedures. S peed indicators must be accurate to ± 3  mph at speeds 
of 10 to 3 0 mph and within ± 5 mph at speeds above 3 0 mph. When an inaccuracy of the speed indicator 
is observed, train speed must be adj usted accordingly, and the exception must be noted on a Crew 
Information Form. Report the occurrence to the train dispatcher.
25 .0 C oup l ing Locomotives for Mul tip l e U nit (MU ) O p eration
To connect locomotives for multiple unit operation:
• Connect the electrical j umper cable between locomotives.
• Couple the corresponding multiple unit hoses.
• Open brake pipe and multiple unit hose angle cocks between locomotives.
• Connect walkway safety chains and lower walkway platform, if equipped.
26 .0 S ep arating Locomotives
When separating locomotives:
• D isconnect walkway safety chains and position the walkway platform, if equipped.
• D isconnect MU  cables .
• Plug the MU  cables into a dummy receptacle or store in other designated locations .
• Close cut out cocks and angle cock.
• Attach air hoses to the dummy couplings or place them in the pockets.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 45
27.0 Locomotive Air Brake Test
27.1 Locomotive Air Brake Test Requirement
Perform a locomotive air brake test when:
• A locomotive consist is first assembled or coupled together.
• Adding locomotive(s) to a consist.
• Removing other than rear locomotive(s) from a consist.
• Changing operating ends.
• The locomotive consist is rearranged.
Locomotive air brake test is not required when taking power from a mechanical facility with 
a completed Locomotive Consist Information Form or notified the test has been previously performed.
27.2 Performing a Locomotive Brake Test
To perform a locomotive air brake test, complete the following:
• Protect the locomotive(s) from unintended movement.
• Ensure a qualified person is positioned on the ground to confirm that all brake cylinders extend 
and retract as intended on the locomotive(s) being tested.
• Place the automatic brake handle in the release position for at least two minutes to ensure the 
locomotive air brake system is fully charged.
• With the independent and automatic brake handles in release, fully apply the independent brake 
and verify all locomotive brakes apply.
• Release the independent brake and verify all locomotive brakes release.
• Make a 15-psi automatic brake reduction and verify all locomotive brakes apply.
• Actuate the independent brake for at least four seconds per locomotive and verify all locomotive 
brakes release.
• Make a further reduction with the automatic brake, no less than full service, and verify all 
locomotive brakes apply.
• Release the automatic brake and verify all locomotive brakes release.
• Test the alerter, except when adding trailing locomotive(s).
28.0 Moving Locomotive(s)
28.1 Prior To Movement
Prior to making an initial movement of a locomotive consist, make a visual inspection to verify:
• Locomotive air brakes are applied on each locomotive.
• Required air hoses are coupled between all locomotives in the consist.
• Cut out cocks and valves are positioned correctly.
• Operational status of locomotives.
• Main reservoir pressure is higher than 105-psi and air brake pressures are within standard.
• Hand brakes are released on all locomotives.
When locomotive status has been documented on a Locomotive Consist Information Form located on 
the lead consist, the locomotive engineer is relieved from performing a visual inspection of the first
five bullet points listed above.

28 .2 Ch anging Operating E nds
When changing operating ends or during the initial movement of a locomotive consist, perform 
the following:
• A fter movement begins and speed is below 1 0 mph, apply the independent brake.
o Ensure brake cylinder pressure develops and speed reduces.
• Release the independent brake and ensure the locomotive(s) roll freely.
• Make a 1 0- psi reduction with the automatic brake.
o Ensure brake cylinder pressure develops and speed reduces.
• A ctuate the independent brake and ensure the locomotive(s) roll freely.
28 .3 Operating Cab  R eq uirem ents
Operate a light locomotive consist from the cab nearest the direction of travel when any of the following 
apply:
• The distance to be traveled ex ceeds two miles.
• A  member of the crew does not control the movement using hand signals or radio.
• V isibility is impaired .
28 .4 Mov ing L ocom otiv e Consists in a Term inal
Multiple locomotive consists may be moved within a terminal area with only the brake pipe connected 
provided:
• Movement does not ex ceed 1 0 mph.
• The automatic brake is used to control speed.
• B rake pipe is connected and angle cocks are open between locomotives .
• A ll locomotives coupled to the controlling locomotive are conditioned properly :
o A utomatic brake valve(s) cut out and in handle off position.
o Independent brake valve(s) in trail and in release position.
• B rake test is performed:
o Make a 1 0- psi automatic brake reduction.
o Ensure brakes apply on all locomotives.
o Release the automatic brake.
o Ensure brakes release on all locomotives.
• Release all hand brakes.
28 .5 H ostling L ocom otiv es
When hostling locomotives with inoperative brakes, a minimum of one locomotive with operative brakes 
must be used per six  locomotives with inoperative brakes.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 47
29.0 Modifying Operating Controls
29.1 Cutting Out Operating Controls
To cut out operating controls:
• Ensure locomotive(s) are secured against unintended movement.
• Move the independent brake handle to full application.
• Make a 20-psi reduction with the automatic brake.
• Center the reverser and remove the handle.
• Place the generator field switch in the off position.
• Disarm the EOT, when required.
• Position headlight switch, if necessary.
• Cut out the automatic brake.
• Move the automatic brake handle to handle off / continuous service.
• Cut out the independent brake.
• Move the independent brake handle to release and ensure brake cylinder pressure is maintained.
• If changing operating controls, immediately proceed to the locomotive to be cut in.
29.2 Cutting In Operating Controls
To cut in operating controls, condition the control stand as follows:
• Move the independent brake handle to full application.
• Cut in the independent brake.
• Move the automatic brake handle to release.
• Check air gauges and verify pressures are within standard.
• Cut in the automatic brake.
• Place the generator field switch in the On position.
• Ensure the engine run switch is in the On position.
• Ensure the control/fuel pump switch is in the On position.
• Conduct required air brake test.
30.0 Traction Motors
30.1 Traction Motor Auto Cut Out
When the locomotive screen indicates that a traction motor has automatically cut out, perform 
the following:
• Report the defect to Mechanical.
• Ensure that all traction motor speed sensors are cut-in/enabled.
• Document defect(s) and speed sensor status on the Crew Information Form.

must be used per six  locomotives with inoperative brakes.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 47
29.0 Modifying Operating Controls
29.1 Cutting Out Operating Controls
To cut out operating controls:
• Ensure locomotive(s) are secured against unintended movement.
• Move the independent brake handle to full application.
• Make a 20-psi reduction with the automatic brake.
• Center the reverser and remove the handle.
• Place the generator field switch in the off position.
• Disarm the EOT, when required.
• Position headlight switch, if necessary.
• Cut out the automatic brake.
• Move the automatic brake handle to handle off / continuous service.
• Cut out the independent brake.
• Move the independent brake handle to release and ensure brake cylinder pressure is maintained.
• If changing operating controls, immediately proceed to the locomotive to be cut in.
29.2 Cutting In Operating Controls
To cut in operating controls, condition the control stand as follows:
• Move the independent brake handle to full application.
• Cut in the independent brake.
• Move the automatic brake handle to release.
• Check air gauges and verify pressures are within standard.
• Cut in the automatic brake.
• Place the generator field switch in the On position.
• Ensure the engine run switch is in the On position.
• Ensure the control/fuel pump switch is in the On position.
• Conduct required air brake test.
30.0 Traction Motors
30.1 Traction Motor Auto Cut Out
When the locomotive screen indicates that a traction motor has automatically cut out, perform 
the following:
• Report the defect to Mechanical.
• Ensure that all traction motor speed sensors are cut-in/enabled.
• Document defect(s) and speed sensor status on the Crew Information Form.

4 8 CP K C |  U nited S tates A ir B rake and Train H andling
30.2 A C  T raction Motor Failure
• Do not cut out traction motors or speed sensors without authoriz ation from Mechanical.
• When a potential A C traction motor failure is identified, stop the movement and inspect for the 
following:
o Wheel skids or shelling. 
o E lectrical burn smell.
o A ny signs of heat damage verified by application of a temperature indicating crayon on the 
j ournal bearings.
o G earcase leaks.
o U nusual noises from traction motors.
• Following inspection, contact Mechanical. R eport any defects noted above and be governed by 
instructions received. Document defects, speed sensor status, and Mechanical instructions the 
Crew Information Form.
30.3 DC  T raction Motor Failure
• When a potential DC traction motor failure is identified, stop the movement, and inspect for the 
following:
o Wheel skids or shelling. 
o E lectrical burn smell.
o A ny signs of heat damage verified by application of a temperature indicating crayon on the 
j ournal bearings.
o G earcase leaks.
o U nusual noises from traction motors.
• Following inspection, contact Mechanical. R eport any defects noted above and be governed by 
instructions received. A ll defects and Mechanical instructions shall be documented on the Crew 
Information Form.
• If a DC traction motor is cut out:
o L ocked axle detection function is disabled must be continually monitored to ensure the 
wheels are rotating freely. 
o E nsure the locomotive is marshalled in the lead consist for observation.
o The locomotive must be set off at the nearest set out point, not to exceed the next daily 
inspection or forward point where repairs can be made, whichever occurs first.
30.4  T emporary  W h eelsets
When a defective traction motor assembly has had the pinion gear cut or has been replaced with a 
temporary wheelset, the traction motor and speed sensor are to be manually cut out for only that position. 
The locomotive must be marshalled in the lead consist and closely monitored to confirm that the wheels 
are rotating freely and are not making any unusual noises. Mechanical will advise of any speed or 
operating restrictions. The Crew Information Form must be updated accordingly.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 49
31.0 Speed Sensors
31.1 Speed Sensor Failure
If Mechanical has confirmed that a traction motor speed sensor failure requires the speed sensor to be 
manually cut out, the locomotive must be marshalled within the lead consist. The identified wheel must be 
continually monitored to confirm that it is rotating freely and not making any unusual noises. The 
locomotive must be set off at the nearest set-off point. The Crew Information Form must be updated 
accordingly.
32.0 Distance Measuring Device
32.1 Distance Measuring Device Requirements
The distance measuring device, also referred to as a counter, allows train crews to determine the location 
of the rear car of a train in relation to a given reference point where the counter is activated. When 
programming the distance measuring device, enter the actual train length of the train. In non-signaled 
territory, add an additional three percent to the total train length. The train length entered into the distance 
measuring device must be updated when the train consist or locomotive(s) are changed. 
Crews must exercise discretion and travel an extra distance if a stopping location, clearance point, signal, 
or other restriction requires. Distance measuring devices must be checked for accuracy against known 
distances, which may include predetermined measured mile locations or other locations specified by 
instruction.

5.4  Leaving a Train Unattended ..............................................................................................53
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 51
1.0 General Requirements
Crew members are responsible for securing unattended equipment with hand brakes. Equipment is 
considered unattended when left in a manner that the brake system of the equipment cannot be readily 
controlled by a qualified person. Employees must not engage in any unrelated tasks while attending 
equipment.
2.0 Hand Brakes
Fully apply hand brakes until the slack is out of the chain and the brake shoes are in contact with the 
wheel. In winter conditions, ensure that braking surfaces are free of ice and snow.
Unless testing for securement, hand brakes must be fully released before moving equipment.
3.0 Testing Hand Brake Effectiveness
To ensure a sufficient number of hand brakes are applied, release all air brakes and allow sufficient time 
for release. Cause or allow the slack to adjust to verify that the number of hand brakes applied are 
sufficient to prevent equipment from moving. This test must be completed before uncoupling or leaving 
equipment unattended.
When unable to test hand brake effectiveness, apply hand brakes as follows:
• On grades from 0 to 0.99%, apply hand brakes to at least 20 percent of cars.
• On grades from 1.0 to 1.29%, apply hand brakes to at least 30 percent of cars.
• On grades from 1.3 to 1.79%, apply hand brakes to at least 50 percent of cars.
• On grades 1.8% or higher, apply hand brakes to at least 65 percent of cars.
• Locomotive hand brakes must not be included in the total hand brake count. If in doubt 
or uncertainty exists as to the number of hand brakes to apply, contact management for 
instructions.
4.0 Securing Equipment Following an Emergency Brake Application 
or Train Braking Issue on Heavy or Mountain Grade
When a train experiences an emergency brake application or train braking issue on heavy or mountain 
grade, the following will apply:
• Immediately secure equipment with hand brakes prior to attempting to recharge the air brake 
system.
• At minimum, apply hand brakes in accordance with the following:
o On grades from 1.0 to 1.29%, apply hand brakes to at least 30 percent of cars.
o On grades from 1.3 to 1.79%, apply hand brakes to at least 50 percent of cars.
o On grades 1.8% or higher, apply hand brakes to at least 65 percent of cars.
• Once the air brake system is fully recharged, prior to the release of hand brakes, make an 
automatic brake application sufficient to hold the train.
