5 .3 T rain Check
5 .3.1 T rain Check  R eq uirem ents
The train check feature verifies that the brake pipe is open and unrestricted between the lead and the 
remote consist(s).
A train check is required in the following situations:
• Prior to movement anytime the train has been stopped or it is suspected or known that the train’ s 
brake pipe has been compromised.
Train checks are not required when:
• Brief stops are made to comply with signal indications or to line switches.
• On ascending or descending grades where train handling techniques require automatic air brakes 
to remain applied when initiating movement.
• Immediately following a flow sensor test.
• After building, conditioning, and performing an air brake test at the initial terminal, provided the 
train departs immediately after the brakes are released.
5 .3.2 T rain Check  Procedure
Perform a Train Check as follows:
• E nsure the train is stopped.
• Make the required automatic brake reduction:
o When a Class III air brake test is not required, make at least a 10 - psi reduction.
o When a Class III air brake test is required, make a 2 0 - psi reduction and validate that brake 
pipe pressure has decreased at the rear of the train.
• Wait for service exhaust to cease.
• F rom the S ystem display :
o S elect Train Check .
o S elect E xecute .
• V erify that the remote brake valves are cut out by manually checking status or observing screen 
prompts to perform a brake release.
• When ready to depart, move the automatic brake handle to release.
If the train check is successful, the locomotive screen will show Train Check- OK . If the display shows 
Train Check F ail, inspect the brake pipe for closed angle cocks, brake pipe blockage, or excessive 
leakage, and perform an additional train check. If the subsequent attempt fails, contact the proper 
authority be governed by their instructions. In all circumstances, brake pipe continuity must be validated 
before the train proceeds.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 93
6.0 Distributed Power Operation
6.1 Synchronous Operation
After a distributed power train has been conditioned and the system has been placed in Run mode, all 
remote locomotives will operate in the front group and will reproduce the same commands as the lead 
locomotive. This is considered synchronous operation.
Where possible, operate all remotes in the front group when the train is operating on:
• Near level or gentle undulating grades.
• Continuous descending or ascending grades without severe undulation.
6.2 Asynchronous Operation
Asynchronous operation occurs when a remote consist is controlled independently from the lead 
locomotive. Asynchronous operation requires the distributed power system to be in Run mode. 
The following applies to asynchronous operation:
• Only the consist(s) displayed in the back group will respond to throttle and dynamic brake 
commands initiated from the summary screen.
• Only the consist(s) operating in the front group will respond to commands made from the lead 
locomotive control stand.
6.2.1 Beginning Asynchronous Operation
To utilize asynchronous operation, move the remote consist(s) into the back group to provide 
independent control of the throttle or dynamic braking as follows:
• Press Control Menu (if displayed).
• Press Move to Back.
• On the DP operation screen, verify that a green vertical bar (fence) separates the front and back 
group.
o Remotes to the left of the of the green vertical bar are in the front group.
o Remotes to the right of the green vertical bar are in the back group.
Important considerations:
• If the remote consists were operating in power or dynamic braking (synchronous) when the rear 
remote consist was moved to the back group, the rear remote will remain at its present power 
setting until it is changed using the soft keys on the summary screen.
• If the consists were in Idle when the rear remote consist was moved to the back group, it is 
necessary to select Throttle/Traction or Dyn/Brake and to execute the command to take 
independent control of the back group.
• Once executed, the throttle or dynamic brake will move to Position 1.
• The summary screen continues to display both the front and back throttle positions.
• A remote consist moved to a new group will immediately begin changing throttle or dynamic 
brake positions to match its new group assignment.
• The distributed power system will not allow the back group to operate in dynamic brake if the front 
group is in traction.

Utilize the following to control lead and remote consist(s) during asynchronous operation:

• Control remote consist(s) in the back group by pressing more or less Traction/Braking.
• Control the throttle or braking of the locomotive(s) in the front group, with the control stand of the 
lead locomotive.
6.3  U ncou pling Lead and Remote Locomotive( s)  W ith  or W ith ou t Cars
To uncouple a lead locomotive from a remote consist that will be left standing:
• Stop the train.
• Fully apply the independent brake.
• Make an automatic brake reduction sufficient to prevent movement.
• From the Remote Menu:
o Select each remote to be left standing and one at a time.
 Press BV  Out .
 Press Setout (S/O).
 Press Execute.
• Ensure each remote reports:
o Flow Out.
o Setout.
o Brake Cylinder 7 2 -psi.
• Advise the crew member when it is okay to close the angle cock on the portion to 
be moved.
• The standing portion of the train must be left in emergency.
• V erify that each remote being left reports:
o Brake Pipe 0-psi.
o Brake Cylinder 45-psi (or higher).
o PC Alarm (flashing).
6.4 Cou pling Lead and Remote Locomotive( s)  W ith  or W ith ou t Cars
To return remotes to Normal after Recoupling:
• Fully apply the independent brake.
• Make the required automatic brake reduction:
o On heavy or mountain grades or any grade where locomotive brakes are not sufficient to 
prevent train movement, make at least a 3 5- psi reduction with the automatic brake.
o On grades other than heavy or mountain grade, if train movement can be prevented with the 
locomotive brakes only, no reduction is required.
• From the Remote display:
o Select each remote one at a time.
o Press Normal.
o Press Execute.
• Slowly open the brake pipe angle cock and allow brake pipe pressure to equalize.
• Move the automatic brake handle to release.
• Ensure each remote displays a value for Flow and PCS alarm indicators extinguish.
• V erify that pressure is rising at the rear of the train.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 95
6.5 Break-in-Two
When a break-in-two occurs on a distributed power train, perform the following:
• Select each remote on at a time.
• Press Setout (S/O).
• Press Execute.
• Ensure each remote reports:
o Brake Pipe 0-psi.
o Brake Cylinder 45-psi or higher.
o PCS alarm.
• Determine which remote(s) are still couple to the lead unit and apply sufficient hand brakes to 
secure both portion of the train as required.
• Close the angle cock on the lead portion of the train and recover emergency on the lead unit and 
remote(s) coupled to the lead locomotive.
• If necessary, remove or repair the equipment that cause the emergency application.
• Recouple the train.
6.6 Emergency and Penalty Brake Application Recovery
To recover from an emergency application:
• Secure the train, if necessary.
• For an emergency application:
o Place the automatic brake handle in emergency.
o When prompted by the locomotive display, move the automatic brake handle to Handle Off 
and then Suppression.
• For a penalty application:
o Place the automatic brake handle in suppression for 8 seconds.
o Ensure the PCS indicator is extinguished on the lead locomotive.
• Press the More Menu.
• Press Remote Menu.
• Select each remote one at a time.
• Press Normal.
• Press Execute.
• On the DP screen ensure:
o PCS alarm indicator is extinguished.
o Each remote displays a value for flow.
o BP is rising at the rear of the train.
• After the air brake system is recharged, if necessary, a brake pipe reduction sufficient to prevent 
train movement must be made prior to releasing hand brakes.
6.7 Slow Speed Control
To utilize slow speed control, perform the following:
AC4400 Locomotives
• Place the throttle in Idle.
• Center the reverser.

sections.title: 9 6 CPK C |  United States Air Brake and Train H andling
sections.text:
9 6 CPK C |  United States Air Brake and Train H andling
• Fully apply the independent brake.
• Release the automatic brake.
• On the locomotive screen:
o Select Distr Power.
o Select DP Main.
o Select Mode.
o Select Speed.
o Press Execute.
• Adj ust the speed using Speed Up and Speed Down keys.
• Place the reverser in forward and throttle in Traction 1 .
• Release the independent brake.
• The distributed power system will now control the power to obtain the desired speed 
automatically;  if train moves too quickly, apply up to 1 0 -psi with the independent brake.
• If a stop is requested, place the throttle in Idle.
• To resume, place the throttle in Traction 1 .
• To end slow speed:
o Place the throttle in Idle.
o Select Idle in the mode screen.
E S 4 4 AC Locomotives
• Place the throttle in Idle.
• Center the reverser.
• Fully apply the independent brake.
• Release the automatic brake.
• From the main operating screen:
o Select Speed Control.
o Select Slow Speed.
• Adj ust the speed using Speed Up and Speed Down keys.
• Press Slow Speed On to active the system.
• Place the reverser in the desired direction, release the independent brake, and place the throttle 
in Traction 1 .
• The distributed power system will now control the power to obtain the desired speed 
automatically;  if train moves too quickly, apply up to 1 0 -psi with the independent brake.
• If a stop is requested, place the throttle in Idle.
• To resume, place the throttle in Traction 1 .
• To end slow speed control:
o Place the throttle in Idle.
o Select Slow Speed Off from the locomotive screen.
Regardless of locomotive type, the distributed power remote mode will override the Speed 
Control mode. If a remote was placed in Idle or Isolate, it will remain in this state during speed control 
operation. 
6.8  Tower Control
Tower mode is used at certain facilities to allow tower control of a train. Once tower mode is active, the 
distributed power system will remain in Idle until the tower takes control.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 97
To activate Tower mode:
• Press DP Main.
• Press Mode.
• Press Tower.
• Press Execute.
• Follow on-screen prompts to place the automatic brake to full service and independent brake to 
release.
• Remove the reverser.
• Place the Generator Field breaker to off.
• Advise tower personnel that the train has been set to Tower mode.
To deactivate Tower mode:
• Ensure the train has a Full Service or Penalty Brake application in effect.
o If not, the tower still has control.
• Press DP Main.
• Press Mode.
• Select Idle.
• Select Run.
• Press Execute.
• Charge the air brake system and perform the required air brake test(s).
6.9 Leaving a Train or Locomotive(s) Unattended
To leave a train or locomotives unattended, complete the following:
• Secure the train as required.
• On the locomotive screen:
o Press Distr Power.
o Press DP Main.
o Press Mode.
o Select Idle.
o Select Exit.
• Ensure the Engine Control Switch of lead and remote consist(s) are left on Run.
• Condition locomotives as required.
6.10 Remote Independent Application and Release
• When the independent brake on the lead locomotive is moved to the desired position, the 
command will be sent to the remote locomotives provided it is not in Set Out mode. 
7.0 Distributed Power Restrictions
7.1 Distributed Power Locomotives Coupled to Lead Consist 
Unless authorized by Operations, distributed power locomotives must not be coupled to the lead consist 
of a train. When authorized, ensure:
• Dynamic brake does not exceed allowable limits.
• Brake pipe and main reservoir hoses are coupled between the lead and remote consists.
C P K C  |  U n i t e d  S t a t e s A i r  B r a ke  a n d  T r a i n  H a n d l i n g96

sections.title: 98 CP K C |  U nited S tates Air B rake and Train H andling
sections.text:
98 CP K C |  U nited S tates Air B rake and Train H andling
• When all operating locomotives, including remotes, are located on the headend, the train 
complies with conventional train TrAM req uirements .
• All automatic brake valves, except the lead locomotive, are cut out.
• Trip Optimiz er is not used.
7 .2 O perating  Restrictions – M ix ed Distributed Power T rains
E xcept for trains operated by E nergy Management or when authoriz ed by local operating instruction, the 
following req uirements apply to distributed power operations with mixed distributed power trains:
• While in asynchronous operation, remote locomotive(s) must use the same or lower throttle 
position as the lead locomotive consist.
o E xception: When operating a heavy train on ascending grade, the throttle position of the 
remote(s) may be higher than the lead locomotive consist. Locomotive engineers must be 
vigilant to ensure acceptable in-train force levels are maintained.
• When dynamic brake is used on the lead consist, do not use throttle position(s) on remote 
locomotives.
7 .3 M ax imum Distances B etween Locomotive Consists
If combined air flow to the brake pipe does not exceed 6 0 CF M, the maximum distance between the lead 
and remote consist is 10,000 feet.
If combined air flow to the brake pipe is between 6 1 and 90 CF M and no more than 6 0 CF M at any one 
locomotive consist, the maximum distance between any of the locomotive consists is:
• S ingle Remote Trains: 5500 feet .
• Multiple Remote Trains: 7 500 feet.
7 .4  H andl ing  Dead or Disabl ed Remote Locomotives on Rear of  T rain
In the event a remote locomotive becomes dead or disabled enroute, the train must be conventionaliz ed 
or remarshalled at the first available location. The train may proceed to an alternate location, provided the 
following conditions are met:
• Communication is maintained between lead and remote consists.
• Remote locomotives are set to Isolate mode with the remote feed valve cut out.
• Main Reservoir pressure on the remote is 8 5- psi or greater.
• Train passes a TrAM check.
• The dead or disabled locomotive is drained, if req uired.
When a remote locomotives main reservoir pressure is depleted, the locomotive brakes will be 
inoperative.  
If the main reservoir pressure drops below 8 5 -psi or sustained communication loss occurs with the 
remote, the movement must not exceed 2 5 MP H  and proceed only to the first available location where the 
train can be conventionaliz ed or locomotives replaced.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 99
8.0 Distributed Power Communication
8.1 Distributed Power Communication Check
The distributed power system checks radio and onboard computer communication of the lead and remote 
locomotives. If a communication check fails, the system will:
• Attempt to operate the lead and remote backup radios.
• Declare a communication interruption at the lead and at the remote consist.
8.2 Lead Locomotive Communication Interruption
If a lead locomotive fails to receive an expected command reply from a remote locomotive, a yellow 
COMM light will illuminate or COMM light will flash. 
The lead unit will declare a communication interruption:
• If no reply is received from a remote unit for 45 seconds; or
• In 10 seconds, following an automatic brake pipe reduction.
When a communication interruption is declared, a red COMM light will appear and a double chime will 
sound.
The status displayed for the remote consists will not change during the COMM interruption and will 
continue to indicate the remote status at the time of the failure.
8.3 Remote Locomotive Communication Interruption
If communication loss with remote locomotives occurs, each remote consist will:
• Continue to operate on the last throttle and air brake command received via the radio.
• If no change in brake pipe pressure is detected at the remote, the remote locomotive(s) will:
o Continue to act on the last command received for up to 90 minutes.
o At the end of the 90-minute override, initiate a penalty brake application if radio 
communication has not been reestablished.
The remote brake valve must be cut in and charging at the time of and during the communication 
interruption to allow the remote consist to operate in override. If a remote brake valve is cut out, remote 
will immediately go to idle in the event of a COMM interruption. Certain locomotives will retain dynamic 
braking effort regardless of brake valve condition. Locomotive engineers must monitor gauges to assess 
dynamic brake status. Remote consists must be returned to normal after COMM has been reestablished. 
If possible, during a communications interruption between the lead and remote consists, keep the train 
moving to a location where communications might improve. If distributed power is needed, avoid making 
an automatic brake application.
C P K C  |  U n i t e d  S t a t e s A i r  B r a ke  a n d  T r a i n  H a n d l i n g98

1 02 C PK C  |  U nited States Air B rake and Train Handling
1 .0 HOT - EOT System Setu p
1 .1  Installation
• The calibration date shown on the EOT device must not be expired. 
• Install the EOT
• F rom the EOT display, verify that the EOT battery voltage is 1 2 .2 V or higher.
• Enter the EOT number in the HOT on the lead locomotive.
• Press the HOT COMM TEST button and verify on the HOT display that the C omm Test passed.
• After charging the train, validate that the pressure displayed on the HOT is within + / - 3 psi of the 
EOT pressure.
1 .2  Repeating
• On trains equipped with a mid-train train distributed power locomotive, configure the HOT 
repeater as follows:  
o DPS Device – Ensure the HOT is disarmed and the EOT ID is set to z ero.
o Integrated LX A – Enter the EOT ID into the HOT. 
o Q uantum Q 3442  – Enter the EOT ID and place the toggle switch in the repeater position.
2 .0 Arming the HOT
To arm the HOT:
• Press the button on the EOT.
• When the Arming message appears on the HOT, immediately press the Arm button on the HOT.
• Verify that the HOT indicates Armed or Emergency Enabled.
• If the system fails to Arm, press the HOT C OMM TEST button to determine communication status 
and repeat the steps above.  
3 .0 Testing the HOT and EOT System
An HOT/EOT system must be tested at the initial terminal or other point of installation to determine that 
the device can initiate an emergency brake application. To test the system, perform the following:
• C lose the angle cock ahead of the last car.
• Activate the EOT emergency toggle switch in the locomotive cab. 
• Verify that the cars behind the angle cock go into emergency.
• Allow 1 5  seconds for the EOT emergency valve to close before opening the angle cock.
• Open the angle cock. 
Alternative testing methods:
• Test the system with the EOT mounted on the locomotive. Perform a comm test after installation 
on train.
• Individual components are bench tested by Mechanical. Perform a comm test after installation on 
train.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 103
4.0 Disarming the HOT
To disarm the HOT:
• Initiate the Disarm function on the HOT and set the EOT ID code to “00000”.
• Verify the HOT displays “disarmed” or “emergency disabled” and an EOT ID of 00000.
Disarm the HOT when:
• A train reaches its final terminal.
• Replacing an HOT or EOT enroute.
5.0 Emergency Toggle Switch
The HOT/EOT system must be properly armed to activate an emergency brake application. To initiate an 
EOT emergency brake activation:  
• Lift the red cover and toggle of the EOT emergency switch.
• Verify the rear brake pipe pressure reduces to 0 psi.
When an EOT emergency brake activation is initiated, the HOT will continually transmit a series of 
emergency brake commands to the EOT for two minutes or until the EOT acknowledges the command.  
If, after two minutes, the EOT has not responded and the rear brake pipe pressure is not 0 PSI, the 
locomotive engineer will be required to reinitiate the EOT emergency brake activation.
6.0 Emergency Application Capability from Rear of Train
All trains must have the ability to initiate an emergency brake application from the rear of the train, except:
• Locomotives operating without cars.
• Passenger trains.
• Locals, road switchers, work trains, and yard assignments provided:
o Train weight does not exceed 4,000 trailing tons.
o Movement does not operate over heavy or mountain grade or travel a distance farther than 
can normally be operated by a single crew in a single tour of duty.
• Trains that operate at speeds less than 30 mph and do not operate over heavy or 
mountain grades.
7.0 Acceptable Methods for Initiating Emergency Application at 
Rear of Train
The following methods will fulfil the requirement to initiate an emergency application from the rear of the 
train:
• An operable HOT and EOT which has been armed and tested at the point of installation.
• A Distributed Power locomotive at the rear of the train which is linked to the lead locomotive.
• Helper locomotive(s), caboose, or passenger equipment at the rear of the train provided it is 
equipped with:
o An emergency brake valve.
o An employee with a two-way voice radio in communication with the locomotive engineer in 
the lead locomotive.

1 0 4 C P K C  |  U nited S tates A ir B rak e and Train H andling
8 .0 HOT- EOT S y st em  Enr o u t e F ailu r e ( o r  co nsider  calling t h is “ L o ss 
o f  Em er gency  A p p licat io n C ap ab ilit y  f r o m  R ear  o f  Tr ain” )
8 .1 R eq u ir em ent s 
Trains required to be equipped with rear of train emergency capability are considered to have an enroute 
failure when one of the following conditions occur:
• H OT indicates F ront to R ear communication loss. R ear to F ront communication loss is N OT 
considered an enroute failure.
• EOT is not A rmed or has lost A rmed status on the lead locomotive.
• H OT indicates EOT emergency valve failure.
• H OT indicates EOT dead battery.
• H OT indicates Emergency D isabled
• D istributed power communication loss ex ceeding 1 6  ½  minutes.
• A  loss of voice radio communication between helper locomotive(s), caboose, or passenger 
equipment at the rear of the train and the lead controlling locomotive.
8 .2  R esp o nding t o  an Enr o u t e F ailu r e ( L o ss o f  Em er gency  A p p licat io n C ap ab ilit y )
W hen an enroute failure occurs, trains must not:
• Ex ceed 3 0  mph until the failure is corrected.
• P ick  up cars enroute.
• D escend or move from a stop on heavy or mountain grade as listed in the timetable, unless the 
train is equipped with an alternative method to initiate an emergency brak e application from the 
rear of the train. A lternatives include helper locomotives, occupied cabooses, or radio control 
locomotives. A ll movements must be made under the direction of local management.
9 .0 L o ss o f  C o m m u nicat io n
The EOT/ H OT system utilizes the following parameters for communication loss:
• F ront to R ear – communication loss occurs when the H OT does not receive a response to its 
C omm Test messages from the EOT for 1 6  ½  minutes.
• R ear to F ront – communication loss occurs when an H OT has not received communication from 
the EOT for 5  minutes.
A dditional information:
• H OT/ EOT communication may be restored by moving out of a communication loss area. 
• R ear to F ront communication loss alarm will clear when the H OT receives any message from the 
EOT.
• F ront to R ear communication loss alarms will clear when the H OT receives a response from the 
EOT to a C OM M  Test message.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 105
10.0 Handling EOT Devices
EOT devices may be transported as follows:
• In locomotive EOT holders.
• Installed on the coupler of a distributed power locomotive at the rear of a train.
• In the locomotive’s engine room or other designated locomotive tool compartment, provided the 
EOT device(s) do not create a tripping or other hazard and movement is authorized by 
management.
• Ensure EOT equipment is handled with care to avoid damage to antennas and other internal 
components.

sections.text:
108 CPK C |  United States Air Brak e and Train Handling
1 .0 TrAM Areas
Train Area Marshalling areas are:
• Defined by a combination of grade and curvature.
• Divided into six areas.
• Identified in the subdivision page of the timetable.
2 .0 Trai n  Ty p es
All trains are classified as one of the following:
• Heavy Bulk :
o Contains only conventional cars.
o All cars on the train weigh at least 100 tons and measure 65 feet or less in length.
• Light Bulk :
o Contains only conventional cars.
o All cars on the train weight less than 50 tons and measure 65 feet or less in length.
• Heavy Uniform:
o Contains either conventional or multi-platform cars.
o All cars on the train:
 Weigh at least 50 tons per car or platform.
 The maximum weight difference between cars or platforms does not exceed 20 tons.
 Maximum length difference between cars or platforms is ten feet.
• Mixed:
o Any train that does not qualify as one of the train types listed above.
4 .0 Trai n  C o n f i gu rat i o n s
4 .1  C o n v en t i o n al  Trai n
• A conventional train is a train in which all operating locomotives are located at the head end of a 
train.
• Conventional trains that meet the definition of Heavy Bulk , Light Bulk , or Heavy Uniform must not 
exceed 10,000 feet. Mixed conventional trains must not exceed 10,000 feet or 10,000 tons.
o Exception: Unless otherwise specified, trains with solid intermodal equipment may operate to 
a maximum length of 12,000 feet.
4 .2  D i st ri b u t ed  P o w er Trai n
• A distributed power train is a train in which all operating locomotives are located at the head end 
of the train and in up to three additional positions throughout the train. All locomotives are 
controlled from the head end locomotive consist.
• The maximum length of a distributed power train must not exceed 14,000 feet.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 109
5.0 TrAM Messages
TrAM messages contain the following parts:
• Part 1 – Train Information: provides essential information about the train, including 
train type.
• Part 2 – Caution Messages: Provides warnings, information, and instructions.
• Part 3 – Marshalling Violations: Lists marshalling violations that require correction before a train 
can proceed.
o “All Areas” messages apply to all trains.
o TrAM Area 1-6 messages apply only to specific TrAM areas.
Example:

sections.text:
110 CPK C |  United States Air Brake and Train Handling
6 .0 Verify ing Train Area Marshalling
Supervisors in major yards and terminals are responsible for compliance with TrAM rules. 
Train crews are responsible to ensure that there are no marshalling violations applicable to the TrAM 
area(s) they will operate on. All violations must be promptly reported to a supervisor and train dispatcher.
Check the following:
• Train consist:
o Consist header messages.
o Car information messages.
o Train statistics messages.
o Dangerous commodity messages.
o Part 1, 2, and 3  Train Area Marshalling messages.
• Crew Information form for work performed enroute.
If there are no marshalling violations the train may proceed complying with all caution messages.
7 .0 TrAM Check Req uirements for W ork Performed Enroute
7 .1 Conventional Trains
The following will govern TrAM check requirements for conventional trains performing 
work enroute. 
H eavy  B ulk Trains:
• Not required for setout or pickup of operating locomotive(s).
• Not required for setout of cars.
• Not required for pick up of cars that meet the criteria of a Heavy Bulk train.
Light B ulk :
• Not required for setout or pickup of operating locomotive(s).
• Not required for setout of cars.
• Not required for pickup of cars that meet the criteria of a Light Bulk train.
H eavy  Uniform :
• Not required for setout or pickup of operating locomotive(s).
• Not required for setout of cars.
• Requirements for a Mix ed Conventional train apply when picking up cars .
7 .2  Distributed Power Trains
Ex cept for Heavy Bulk trains originating at a customer facility, distributed power trains must always 
receive a TrAM check after equipment is picked up or set out of the train. 
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 111
8.0 Documenting Pickups and Setouts
The following requirements apply after performing work enroute:
Planned pickup or setout:
• Leave updated documents with the train.

Supervisors in major yards and terminals are responsible for compliance with TrAM rules.

Tonnage violation.

excluding operating locomotives, exceeds the threshold tonnage, Maximum Trailing Car Tonnage and 
Ascending Grade Weight Zone rules will apply.

Rem ote Consist
The distance between the lead locomotive and last remote consist must not exceed 14,0 0 0  feet. 
Distributed power trains operating with a remote more than 10 ,0 0 0  feet from the lead locomotive must 
operate in a multiple remote configuration or move a remote to a mid-train position.
13 .0 Dy nam ic Brak e
TrAM will determine the maximum allowable dynamic brake for on distributed power trains. Restrictions 
listed will be based on thousands of pounds per the effort indicator on the 
locomotive display.
One of the following messages will be displayed:
• DY N AMIC BRAK E N OT RESTRICTED
• DY N AMIC BRAK E RESTRICTED – DO N OT EXCEED nnn K LBS RETARDIN G FORCE 
14 .0 Rem ote Zones
On Mixed distributed power trains, the cars immediately ahead of the remote locomotive consist(s) will 
form remote zones. TrAM will analyze the equipment ahead of each remote location and display one of 
the following:
• The train passes remote zone marshaling.
• Specific cars have failed remote zone marshaling.
• Remote zone rules do not apply.
Remote zone rules do not apply to a Mixed Distributed Power train when the following conditions are met:
• All cars on the train, except cars on the extreme head end, meet the conditions of a Light Bulk 
train.
o The " extreme head end"  in this case includes all cars up to and including the car furthest from 
the head end that does not meet the conditions of a Light Bulk train.
• The number of cars or platforms on the extreme head end does not exceed 10  percent of the total 
number of cars or platforms between the lead and first remote locomotive consist.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 115
Light Bulk trains that require buffer car(s) will generate failed remote zone marshalling messages. 
Provided a maximum of two loaded buffer cars are positioned on either side of the locomotive, the remote 
zone marshalling violation can be disregarded. 
If a rear remote consist is removed, a maximum of two loaded buffers may be left on the rear of 
the train.
15.0 Buff and Draft Forces on Distributed Power Trains
When TrAM determines that draft or buff forces are exceeded, TrAM will display one of the following 
messages:
• DRAFT FORCES EXCEED MAXIMUM LEAD REMOTE 1 REMOTE 2 REMOTE 3
• BUFF FORCES EXCEED MAXIMUM REMOTE 1 REMOTE 2 REMOTE 3
16.0 Ascending Grade Weight Zone (AGWZ) Rules
AGWZ rules apply to TrAM areas 4 and 5. The combination of ascending grade and curvature can create 
undesirable in-train forces that affect lighter weight cars under certain operating conditions. AGWZ rules 
do not apply to Heavy Bulk trains. 
16.1 Conventional Trains
The following AGWZ requirements apply to conventional trains:
• Light Bulk:
o Less than 24 driving axles:
 AGWZ restrictions do not apply.
o More than 24 driving axles:
 Weight does not exceed TrAM area Threshold Tonnage:
• AGWZ restrictions do not apply.
 Weight is greater than TrAM area Threshold Tonnage:
• Prohibited.
• Mixed and Heavy Uniform:
o Less than 24 driving axles:
 AGWZ restrictions do not apply.
o More than 24 driving axles:
 Weight does not exceed TrAM area Threshold Tonnage:
• AGWZ restrictions do not apply.
 Weight is greater than TrAM area Threshold Tonnage:
• Cars or Platforms on head end of train must pass the minimum requirements listed in 
Conventional Train Head End Weight Requirements.
Train crews are responsible to ensure that Heavy Uniform conventional trains do not operate with AGWZ 
rule violations. TrAM will not generate messages for this train type.
16.2 Distributed Power Trains
The following AGWZ requirements apply to distributed power trains:
• If TrAM does not display messages indicating that Draft or Buff force have been exceeded, the 
train complies with AGWZ rules.

16 .3 Conventional T rain H ead End W eight Req u irements
Cars or platforms on the head end of Mixed Conventional trains affected by AGWZ rules are restricted as 
follows:
• TrAM Area 4:
o First 10 cars or platforms must each weigh a minimum of 60 tons.
• TrAM area 5:
o First 12 cars or platforms must each weigh a minimum of 75 tons; or
o First 15 cars or platforms must each weigh a minimum of 60 tons.
When an articulated or solid drawbar connected car extends beyond the first 10, 12, or 15 cars or 
platforms required by this rule, the minimum weight rules apply to each platform on the car.
17 .0 T rA M Messages and Crew  Responsibility 
Train Area Marshaling Messages for Areas 4 and 5 will indicate, for Mixed Conventional trains only, if the 
cars or platforms on the extreme head end of the train meet the minimum weight requirements for 
operation with over 24 equivalent driving axles in an Ascending Weight Zone.
Train Area Marshalling messages will indicate if the cars on the head end of the train meet the minimum 
requirements for operation with more than 24 equivalent driving axles in Ascending Grade Weight Zones 
in TrAM Areas 4 and 5.
When operating in an Ascending Grade Weight Zone, crews are responsible to ensure that the number of 
equivalent driving axles of their train does not cause a violation of the Ascending Grade Weight Zone 
Rules. TrAM messages do NOT state if the train is operating with too many equivalent driving axles for 
that train configuration in an Ascending Grade Weight Zone.

1 . 0  R esponsib ilities of Certified Employees
Locomotive engineers, remote control operators, and conductors must:
• Comply with all certification requirements.
• E nsure driving record and vision and hearing information is submitted within required timelines.
• K now the expiration date of their certification.
• N otify local management no less than 1 4  days prior to expiration of their certification.
• N otify crew management within 4 8  hours of expiration of their certification.
• N ot work or accept a call to work a certified position beyond their certification expiration date.
• Carry a current certification card or temporary certificate while on duty.
• Present their certification card to the proper authority upon request.
• Be qualified on the territory over which they will operate.
• Complete a territory exam for each territory over which a qualification will be held:
o D uring each recertification cycle.
o W hen first qualifying over a territory.
o Before operating over a territory for which a qualification has lapsed.
2 . 0  M otor Veh icle D riving R ecords
Locomotive engineers, remote control operators, and conductors must report any convictions for:
• O perating a motor vehicle while under the influence of or impaired by a controlled substance .
• R efusal to undergo such testing when a law enforcement official seeks to find out whether a 
person is operating under the influence of alcohol or a controlled substance.
State sponsored diversion programs, guilty pleas, and completed state actions to cancel, revoke, 
suspend, or deny a driver’ s license are considered as applied to this rule.
An employee must report any conviction to an employee assistance representative and the M anager 
O perating Practices within 4 8  hours after the employee receives notice of a conviction. M anagers notified 
of a conviction by an employee must also report this information to the O perating Practices. 
3 . 0  Familiariz ation
The following general requirements will apply to territory familiarization:
• F ederal submissions for CF R  2 4 0  and CF R  2 4 2  will govern familiarization standards.
• A locomotive engineer not qualified on a specific territory will be provided a minimum of one 
round trip with a locomotive engineer pilot.
• A conductor not qualified on a specific territory will be provided a minimum of one round trip with 
a qualified pilot.
• A locomotive engineer or conductor who has not operated over a territory for a period of twelve 
consecutive months must make a minimum of one familiarization trip.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 119
Glossary
Accelerometer: An instrument that displays in mph per minute the rate of speed increase or decrease.
AC Locomotive: Locomotives equipped with AC traction motors that are not affected by short time 
ratings.
Actuate: Action required to prevent an automatic brake application on the locomotive(s) or to release 
locomotive brakes from an automatic brake application.
Air Brake: A system of devices operated by compressed air arranged in a system and controlled 
manually, electronically, or pneumatically, that retards or arrests the motion of a car or locomotive.
Air Brake System: A collection of devices required for the operating air brakes to control the speed of 
and stop a locomotive or train.
Air Compressor: A locomotive device, powered by the diesel engine or an electric motor, that 
compresses air for operating the air brakes and all other air-operated devices on locomotives 
and cars.
Air Flow Indicator: An instrument that measures the air flow through the automatic brake valve to the 
brake pipe.
Air Gauge: An instrument that indicates air pressure in pounds per square inch (PSI).
Alerter: A device that initiates a penalty brake application when the locomotive engineer does not 
maintain the required frequency of movements of the controls.
Angle Cock: A device used to open and close the brake pipe on the ends of locomotives and cars.
Articulated Car: A car constructed by permanently connecting two or more platforms with an articulated 
joint.
Automatic Brake Valve: A device that controls the flow of main reservoir air into the equalizing reservoir 
and brake pipe to charge and release brakes.
Automatic Brake Valve Cut Out Valve: A device used to cut the automatic brake in or out.
“B” End: The end of a freight car where the hand brake is located, unless otherwise identified.
Bleed: A term used to describe the venting of air to atmosphere on a car by manual operation of the 
release valve.
Block of Cars: Two or more cars coupled together that have previously received a Class I or Class IA air 
brake test for which the Train Brake Status is available.
Block Swap: Adding a maximum of one car or solid block of cars, qualified by the required air brake test 
and safety inspection, to another through train.
Brake Application: A brake pipe pressure reduction that causes the control valve to move to the service 
or emergency position.

sections.text:
1 1 8 CPK C |  U nited States Air Brake and Train H andling
1 . 0  R esponsib ilities of Certified Employees
Locomotive engineers, remote control operators, and conductors must:
• Comply with all certification requirements.
• E nsure driving record and vision and hearing information is submitted within required timelines.
• K now the expiration date of their certification.
• N otify local management no less than 1 4  days prior to expiration of their certification.
• N otify crew management within 4 8  hours of expiration of their certification.
• N ot work or accept a call to work a certified position beyond their certification expiration date.
• Carry a current certification card or temporary certificate while on duty.
• Present their certification card to the proper authority upon request.
• Be qualified on the territory over which they will operate.
• Complete a territory exam for each territory over which a qualification will be held:
o D uring each recertification cycle.
o W hen first qualifying over a territory.
o Before operating over a territory for which a qualification has lapsed.
2 . 0  M otor Veh icle D riving R ecords
Locomotive engineers, remote control operators, and conductors must report any convictions for:
• O perating a motor vehicle while under the influence of or impaired by a controlled substance .
• R efusal to undergo such testing when a law enforcement official seeks to find out whether a 
person is operating under the influence of alcohol or a controlled substance.
State sponsored diversion programs, guilty pleas, and completed state actions to cancel, revoke, 
suspend, or deny a driver’ s license are considered as applied to this rule.
An employee must report any conviction to an employee assistance representative and the M anager 
O perating Practices within 4 8  hours after the employee receives notice of a conviction. M anagers notified 
of a conviction by an employee must also report this information to the O perating Practices. 
3 . 0  Familiariz ation
The following general requirements will apply to territory familiarization:
• F ederal submissions for CF R  2 4 0  and CF R  2 4 2  will govern familiarization standards.
• A locomotive engineer not qualified on a specific territory will be provided a minimum of one 
round trip with a locomotive engineer pilot.
• A conductor not qualified on a specific territory will be provided a minimum of one round trip with 
a qualified pilot.
• A locomotive engineer or conductor who has not operated over a territory for a period of twelve 
consecutive months must make a minimum of one familiarization trip.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 119
Glossary
Accelerometer: An instrument that displays in mph per minute the rate of speed increase or decrease.
AC Locomotive: Locomotives equipped with AC traction motors that are not affected by short time 
ratings.
Actuate: Action required to prevent an automatic brake application on the locomotive(s) or to release 
locomotive brakes from an automatic brake application.
Air Brake: A system of devices operated by compressed air arranged in a system and controlled 
manually, electronically, or pneumatically, that retards or arrests the motion of a car or locomotive.
Air Brake System: A collection of devices required for the operating air brakes to control the speed of 
and stop a locomotive or train.
Air Compressor: A locomotive device, powered by the diesel engine or an electric motor, that 
compresses air for operating the air brakes and all other air-operated devices on locomotives 
and cars.
Air Flow Indicator: An instrument that measures the air flow through the automatic brake valve to the 
brake pipe.
Air Gauge: An instrument that indicates air pressure in pounds per square inch (PSI).
Alerter: A device that initiates a penalty brake application when the locomotive engineer does not 
maintain the required frequency of movements of the controls.
Angle Cock: A device used to open and close the brake pipe on the ends of locomotives and cars.
Articulated Car: A car constructed by permanently connecting two or more platforms with an articulated 
joint.
Automatic Brake Valve: A device that controls the flow of main reservoir air into the equalizing reservoir 
and brake pipe to charge and release brakes.
Automatic Brake Valve Cut Out Valve: A device used to cut the automatic brake in or out.
“B” End: The end of a freight car where the hand brake is located, unless otherwise identified.
Bleed: A term used to describe the venting of air to atmosphere on a car by manual operation of the 
release valve.
Block of Cars: Two or more cars coupled together that have previously received a Class I or Class IA air 
brake test for which the Train Brake Status is available.
Block Swap: Adding a maximum of one car or solid block of cars, qualified by the required air brake test 
and safety inspection, to another through train.
Brake Application: A brake pipe pressure reduction that causes the control valve to move to the service 
or emergency position.

sections.title: 1 2 0 CPKC |  U nited States Air B rake and Train Handling
sections.text:
1 2 0 CPKC |  U nited States Air B rake and Train Handling
Brake C ylinder: A metallic cylinder containing a piston. Compressed air forces the piston outward to 
apply the brakes. When the air pressure is released, the piston returns to its normal position by a release 
spring coiled around the piston rod inside the cylinder.
Brake C ylinder Release Valve: The valve that initially bleeds brake cylinder pressure. I f held open, it will 
bleed auxiliary and emergency reservoir pressures.
Brake I ndicator: A device which indicates the brake application range and indicates whether brakes are 
applied and released.
Brake Pipe: The pipe, angle cocks, hoses, and hose couplings that distribute compressed air throughout 
the automatic brake system.
Brake Pipe Gradient: The difference in brake pipe pressure between the locomotive or air source and 
the rear car of the train. 
Branch  Pipe C ut out C ock: A device on locomotives and cars that isolates the control valve from 
the brake pipe.
Brake Pipe Pressure: The amount of pressure contained in the brake pipe, commonly expressed in 
pounds per square inch (psi).
Buff Force: Compressive coupler forces that occur during a slack-bunched condition.
C ommunication Loss I dle Down: A distributed power feature that detects a change in brake pipe 
pressure during an interruption of distributed power radio communication. Also referred to as Comm L oss 
I dle D own.  
C ontinuity: The ability to transmit a brake signal between the lead locomotive and the last piece of 
equipment on the train.
C ontrol Valve: The valve on locomotives and cars that charges reservoirs and applies or releases brake 
cylinder pressure in response to changes in brake pipe pressure.
C oupler Alignment C ontrol: Specially equipped couplers, installed on most locomotives that only allow 
the coupler in buff to move laterally within certain limits.
C ut Out C ock or Valve: A device used to cut in or cut out certain air brake functions.
C ycle Braking: The process of applying, releasing, and reapplying train brakes to control speed without 
completely recharging the train brake system.
DC  Locomotive: L ocomotives equipped with D C traction motors.
Dead Engine C ut Out : A device near the locomotive control valve used when a locomotive unit is 
handled dead-in-train. When the dead engine cut out cock is opened, the number 2  main reservoir is 
charged from the brake pipe to operate the locomotive brakes.
Dead- in- C onsist: A method of transporting a locomotive unit or units with the diesel engine not running 
but coupled to an operating unit.
Dead- in- Tow: Hauling locomotive(s) in a train with the brake pipe coupled and the M U  air hoses 
uncoupled.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 121
Distributed Power: One or more locomotive consists that are remotely controlled from the lead, 
locomotive.
Draft Force: Pulling force, or tension on couplers and draft gear during a slack-stretched condition.
Draft Gear: A cushioning device that transmits draft or buff forces between the coupler and the car or 
locomotive frame.
Driving Axle: A locomotive axle used for tractive effort.
Dynamic Brake: The system that electronically converts energy created by the momentum of a moving 
locomotive into an effective retarding brake.
Dynamic Brake Factor: A numerical value used to convey the dynamic braking capability of 
a locomotive.
Dynamic Brake Holding Feature: A feature of the lead controlling locomotive that allows dynamic 
braking effort when a PCS open condition exists.
Emergency Application: A reduction in brake pipe pressure at a rate sufficient to cause control valves to 
move to the emergency position.
Emergency Brake Valve: A valve used to initiate an emergency brake application.
EOT (End of Train Device): A system of components that determines the rear car brake pipe pressure 
and transmits that information to the display on the head-of-train telemetry device (HOT).
Equalizing Reservoir: A small reference volume on locomotives used to make service brake 
applications. 
False Gradient:
A term that describes the amount of pressure present in the rear car while the 
air brake system is still recharging. False Gradient is any pressure less than True Gradient. The 
amount of False Gradient can be determined by subtracting False Gradient from True Gradient. 
Example:
88-psi – Highest obtainable rear car pressure (True Gradient)
85-psi – current rear car pressure while recharging (False Gradient)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3-psi = Amount of false gradient
Foreign Locomotive: Any locomotive not owned by CPKC.
Foundation Brake Gear: The levers, rods, brake beams, etc. that connect the brake cylinder piston rod 
to the brake shoes. When air pressure forces the piston out, the brake shoes are forced against the 
wheels.
Full Service Application: A service reduction of brake pipe pressure that equalizes the pressure 
between the brake cylinder and the auxiliary reservoir.

sections.title: 1 2 2 C PK C  |  United S tates Air Brake and Train H andling
sections.text:
1 2 2 C PK C  |  United S tates Air Brake and Train H andling
G rade: The slope of railway track. G rades are classified as follows:
• L ight G rade:  any grade below 1 .0 percent
• H eavy G rade:  any grade between 1 .0 and 1 .8  percent
• Mountain G rade:  any grade greater than 1 .8  percent
• Ascending G rade:  A section of track where elevation increases
• C resting G rade:  A long ascending grade which rapidly changes to a long descending grade, both 
of significant magnitude, usually on heavy grade
• D escending G rade:  A section of track where elevation decreases
H and Brake: An assortment of levers, chains, rods, and gears that, when applied by wheel or lever, 
forces the brake shoes against the braking surfaces to control car or locomotive movement.
H OT  (H ead of T rain Device): A telemetry transmitter/ receiver that provides the locomotive engineer with 
the displays and controls needed to monitor and operate the associated end-of-train telemetry device 
( E O T) .
H elper L ocomotive: A locomotive controlled by a helper locomotive engineer used to assist another 
train.
H orsepower per T on (H PT ): The total horsepower of all working locomotives divided by the total trailing 
weight of the train in tons.
Independent Brake: A device used to operate the air brakes on a locomotive independent of the 
automatic brakes.
Initial T erminal: The location where a train is originally assembled.
In- T rain Forces: Any force occurring within a train. E xamples include buff, draft, run- in, and run out.
Isolation Switch: A multiple position switch used to change the operative status of a locomotive.
J ackknifing: When the center sill between two rail vehicles is excessively misaligned or the coupler is 
angled sharply. Usually caused by excessive buff forces.
L inking: The process of electronically connecting a lead locomotive to a remote locomotive on a 
distributed power train.
L ight L ocomotive (s): O ne or more locomotives not coupled to cars.
L oad Current Meter: An instrument that indicates the amount of current, in amps, flowing through a D C
locomotive’s traction motor. Also called an ammeter.
L ocal: A train assigned to perform switching enroute which operates with 4 ,000 trailing tons or less and 
travels between a point of origin and a point of final destination, for a distance that is no greater than that 
which can normally be operated by a single crew in a single tour of duty.
L ocomotive Consist: O ne or more locomotives with multiple unit ( MU)  connectors coupled, cut in, and 
operated from a single point of control.
Main Reservoir: A reservoir on a locomotive that stores, cools, and dries the supply of 
compressed air.
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling 123
Minimum Reduction: A 7-psi automatic brake pipe reduction. 
Multiple Unit (MU) Connections: The hoses and angle cocks at both ends of locomotives that connect 
air brake equipment in a locomotive consist, allowing operation from a single control. MU connections 
include the Brake Pipe, Main Reservoir, Actuating, Independent Application and Release, and electrical 
jumper cable.
Off Air: Not connected to a continuous source of compressed air of at least 60-psi.
Overcharge: When brake equipment on cars or locomotives is charged to a pressure higher than the 
regulating valve setting.
Penalty Brake Application: An automatic brake application at a service rate caused by a safety control 
device, such as an electronic alertness device, overspeed, or foot pedal.
Pneumatic Control Switch (PCS): An air operated switch activated by an emergency or penalty 
brake application that drops the engine speed to idle.
Pressure Maintaining Feature: A system designed to overcome brake pipe leakage in both the release 
and service positions of the automatic brake valve. 
Propagation: The serial action of a brake application from car to car through a train.
Proper Authority: A position that provides managerial oversight of operation. Proper authority varies by 
location and type of operation. 
Quick Service: The local venting of brake pipe pressure at each car. 
Reduction: A decrease of brake pipe pressure at a rate and amount sufficient to initiate or increase an 
automatic brake application.
Reduction Relay Valve: A device on long cars that helps reduce brake pipe pressure during service and 
emergency brake applications. The valve compensates for the added length of brake pipes on long cars.
Regulating Valve: At the automatic brake valve, a device that controls the maximum pressure put into 
the equalizing reservoir and brake pipe. The air controlled is supplied by the locomotive main reservoir 
and delivered to the automatic brake system.
Run In: The rapid change of the train’s coupler slack to a buff state.
Run Out: The rapid change of a train’s coupler slack to a draft state.
Running Release: The release of an automatic brake application while the train is moving.
Safety Control Devices: A variety of safety devices including event recorders, alerters, deadman 
controls, automatic cab signals, cab signal whistles, automatic train stop equipment, and automatic train 
control equipment.
Sag: A descending grade followed by a level, nearly level, or ascending grade. 
Service Brake Application: A reduction of brake pipe pressure at a controlled rate that causes the 
control valve to move to a service position and apply the brakes.

sections.title: 124 CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
sections.text:
124 CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
Slack Action: Movement of part of a coupled train at a speed different from another part of 
the train.
Solid Block of cars: Two or more freight cars coupled together.
Split Reduction: The preferred method of applying train brakes. An initial 7-psi brake pipe reduction 
followed by additional reductions in 2 to 3-psi increments spaced 30 seconds apart. 
Stretch Braking: Slowing or stopping a train using the automatic air brakes and enough power to 
maintain a slack-stretched condition not to exceed throttle 4.
Stringlining: The result of excessive draft forces in a train negotiating a curve. Stringlining causes wheel 
climb, track damage, or derailment.
Throttle Modulation: Adjusting the throttle one notch at a time to control train speed and in-train forces.
Tons per Operative Brake (TOB): The measurement calculated by dividing the gross trailing tonnage of 
a train, not including locomotives, by the total number of cars with operative air brakes.
Tractive Effort: The force exerted by a locomotive on the track to move a train.
Tractive Effort Meter: The device that indicates the tractive effort being produced by a locomotive with 
AC traction motors.
Train Consist: Rail cars coupled together which form a train.
Train Separation: Any unplanned train separation involving mechanical coupling equipment.
True Gradient: a term that describes the point, with the automatic brake released, where the pressure on 
the rear car has stopped rising and the air brake system is fully charged. On distributed power trains, the 
sum of air flow on the lead and cut in remote consists can be used to indicate when a train has reached 
true gradient
Undesired Emergency (UDE): An undesired emergency application of a train’s air brake system.
Undulating Grade: A track profile with frequent grade changes.
Vent Valve: A valve attached to the brake system of a car or locomotive that will vent brake pipe 
pressure in response to an emergency brake application. 
Wheel Slide: When the wheel rotates slower than lengthwise movement.
Wheel Slip: When the wheel rotates faster than lengthwise movement.
Work Train: A non-revenue service train of 4,000 trailing tons or less used for the administration or 
upkeep service of the railroad.
Yard Air: A supply of compressed air in a train yard used to charge and test trains.
C P K C  |  U n i t e d  S t a t e s A i r  B r a ke  a n d  T r a i n  H a n d l i n g124
